benché vi rifiuti come inquilino, venite da me come amico. Considerate la
casa per metà vostra ogni [[motifs/winter|inverno]], e amplieremo le scuderie
secondo il vostro piano migliorato, e con tutte le migliorie del vostro piano
migliorato che vi verranno in mente questa [[motifs/spring|primavera]].”



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_25--part_04" data-title="Mansfield Park — Chapter 25 (part 4)" data-chapter="Chapter 25" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="motif/dance,motif/fire,motif/grave,motif/home,motif/nature,motif/night,motif/time,motif/well,concept/hope,concept/nature,concept/suffering,character/edmund,character/henry_crawford,character/sunday"></span>


“We shall be the losers,” continued Sir Thomas. “His going, though only
eight miles, will be an unwelcome contraction of our family circle; but
I should have been deeply mortified if any son of mine could reconcile
himself to doing less. It is perfectly natural that you should not have
thought much on the subject, Mr. Crawford. But a parish has wants and
claims which can be known only by a clergyman constantly resident, and
which no proxy can be capable of satisfying to the same extent. [[characters/edmund|Edmund]]
might, in the common phrase, do the duty of Thornton, that is, he might
read prayers and preach, without giving up [[works/mansfield-park-(austen)|Mansfield Park]]: he might
ride over every [[characters/sunday|Sunday]], to a house nominally inhabited, and go through
divine service; he might be the clergyman of Thornton Lacey every
seventh day, for three or four hours, if that would content him. But it
will not. He knows that human [[concepts/nature|nature]] needs more lessons than a weekly
sermon can convey; and that if he does not live among his parishioners,
and prove himself, by constant attention, their [[motifs/well|well]]-wisher and friend,
he does very little either for their good or his own.”

Mr. Crawford bowed his acquiescence.

“I repeat again,” added Sir Thomas, “that Thornton Lacey is the only
house in the neighbourhood in which I should _not_ be happy to wait on
Mr. Crawford as occupier.”

Mr. Crawford bowed his thanks.

“Sir Thomas,” said [[characters/edmund|Edmund]], “undoubtedly understands the duty of a
parish priest. We must [[concepts/hope|hope]] his son may prove that _he_ knows it too.”

Whatever effect Sir Thomas’s little harangue might really produce on
Mr. Crawford, it raised some awkward sensations in two of the others,
two of his most attentive listeners—Miss Crawford and Fanny. One of
whom, having never before understood that Thornton was so soon and so
completely to be his [[motifs/home|home]], was pondering with downcast eyes on what it
would be _not_ to see [[characters/edmund|Edmund]] every day; and the other, startled from
the agreeable fancies she had been previously indulging on the strength
of her brother’s description, no longer able, in the picture she had
been forming of a future Thornton, to shut out the church, sink the
clergyman, and see only the respectable, elegant, modernised, and
occasional residence of a man of independent fortune, was considering
Sir Thomas, with decided ill-will, as the destroyer of all this, and
[[concepts/suffering|suffering]] the more from that involuntary forbearance which his
character and manner commanded, and from not daring to relieve herself
by a single attempt at throwing ridicule on his cause.

All the agreeable of _her_ speculation was over for that hour. It was
[[motifs/time|time]] to have done with cards, if sermons prevailed; and she was glad to
find it necessary to come to a conclusion, and be able to refresh her
spirits by a change of place and neighbour.

The chief of the party were now collected irregularly round the [[motifs/fire|fire]],
and waiting the final break-up. William and Fanny were the most
detached. They remained together at the otherwise deserted card-table,
talking very comfortably, and not thinking of the rest, till some of
the rest began to think of them. [[characters/henry-crawford|Henry Crawford]]’s chair was the first
to be given a direction towards them, and he sat silently observing
them for a few minutes; himself, in the meanwhile, observed by Sir
Thomas, who was standing in chat with Dr. Grant.

“This is the assembly [[motifs/night|night]],” said William. “If I were at Portsmouth I
should be at it, perhaps.”

“But you do not wish yourself at Portsmouth, William?”

“No, Fanny, that I do not. I shall have enough of Portsmouth and of
dancing too, when I cannot have you. And I do not know that there would
be any good in going to the assembly, for I might not get a partner.
The Portsmouth girls turn up their noses at anybody who has not a
commission. One might as [[motifs/well|well]] be nothing as a midshipman. One _is_
nothing, indeed. You remember the Gregorys; they are grown up amazing
fine girls, but they will hardly speak to _me_, because Lucy is courted
by a lieutenant.”

“Oh! shame, shame! But never mind it, William” (her own cheeks in a
glow of indignation as she spoke). “It is not worth minding. It is no
reflection on _you_; it is no more than what the greatest admirals have
all experienced, more or less, in their [[motifs/time|time]]. You must think of that,
you must try to make up your mind to it as one of the hardships which
fall to every sailor’s share, like bad weather and hard living, only
with this advantage, that there will be an end to it, that there will
come a [[motifs/time|time]] when you will have nothing of that sort to endure. When you
are a lieutenant! only think, William, when you are a lieutenant, how
little you will care for any nonsense of this kind.”

“I begin to think I shall never be a lieutenant, Fanny. Everybody gets
made but me.”

“Oh! my dear William, do not talk so; do not be so desponding. My uncle
says nothing, but I am sure he will do everything in his power to get
you made. He knows, as [[motifs/well|well]] as you do, of what consequence it is.”

She was checked by the sight of her uncle much nearer to them than she
had any suspicion of, and each found it necessary to talk of something
else.

“Are you fond of dancing, Fanny?”

“Yes, very; only I am soon tired.”

“I should like to go to a ball with you and see you [[motifs/dance|dance]]. Have you
never any balls at Northampton? I should like to see you [[motifs/dance|dance]], and I’d
[[motifs/dance|dance]] with you if you _would_, for nobody would know who I was here,
and I should like to be your partner once more. We used to jump about
together many a [[motifs/time|time]], did not we? when the hand-organ was in the
street? I am a pretty good dancer in my way, but I dare say you are a
better.” And turning to his uncle, who was now close to them, “Is not
Fanny a very good dancer, sir?”

Fanny, in dismay at such an unprecedented question, did not know which
way to look, or how to be prepared for the answer. Some very [[motifs/grave|grave]]
reproof, or at least the coldest expression of indifference, must be
coming to distress her brother, and sink her to the ground. But, on the
contrary, it was no worse than, “I am sorry to say that I am unable to
answer your question. I have never seen Fanny [[motifs/dance|dance]] since she was a
little girl; but I trust we shall both think she acquits herself like a
gentlewoman when we do see her, which, perhaps, we may have an
opportunity of doing ere long.”

“I have had the pleasure of seeing your sister [[motifs/dance|dance]], Mr. Price,” said
[[characters/henry-crawford|Henry Crawford]], leaning forward, “and will engage to answer every
inquiry which you can make on the subject, to your entire satisfaction.
But I believe” (seeing Fanny looked distressed) “it must be at some
other [[motifs/time|time]]. There is _one_ person in company who does not like to have
Miss Price spoken of.”

True enough, he had once seen Fanny [[motifs/dance|dance]]; and it was equally true that
he would now have answered for her gliding about with quiet, light
elegance, and in admirable [[motifs/time|time]]; but, in fact, he could not for the
life of him recall what her dancing had been, and rather took it for
granted that she had been present than remembered anything about her.

He passed, however, for an admirer of her dancing; and Sir Thomas, by
no means displeased, prolonged the conversation on dancing in general,
and was so [[motifs/well|well]] engaged in describing the balls of Antigua, and
listening to what his nephew could relate of the different modes of
dancing which had fallen within his observation, that he had not heard
his carriage announced, and was first called to the knowledge of it by
the bustle of Mrs. Norris.

“Come, Fanny, Fanny, what are you about? We are going. Do not you see
your aunt is going? Quick, quick! I cannot bear to keep good old Wilcox
waiting. You should always remember the coachman and horses. My dear
Sir Thomas, we have settled it that the carriage should come back for
you, and [[characters/edmund|Edmund]] and William.”

Sir Thomas could not dissent, as it had been his own arrangement,
previously communicated to his wife and sister; but _that_ seemed
forgotten by Mrs. Norris, who must fancy that she settled it all
herself.

Fanny’s last feeling in the visit was disappointment: for the shawl
which [[characters/edmund|Edmund]] was quietly taking from the servant to bring and put round
her shoulders was seized by Mr. Crawford’s quicker hand, and she was
obliged to be indebted to his more prominent attention.


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

“Saremo noi i perdenti,” continuò Sir Thomas. “La sua partenza, anche se si tratta di soli otto miglia, rappresenta una riduzione indesiderata del nostro cerchio familiare; ma sarei profondamente offeso se uno dei miei figli fosse disposto a fare di meno. È del tutto naturale che lei non abbia riflettuto molto sull’argomento, signor Crawford. Ma una parrocchia ha bisogni e esigenze che possono essere comprese soltanto da un clero residente stabilmente; nessun sostituto potrebbe soddisfarle nella stessa misura. [[characters/edmund|Edmund]] potrebbe, per usare un’espressione comune, svolgere il ruolo di pastore a Thornton: potrebbe recitare preghiere e predicare, senza abbandonare [[works/mansfield-park-(austen)|Mansfield Park]]; potrebbe recarsi ogni domenica in una casa apparentemente abitata e partecipare alle funzioni religiose. Potrebbe essere il clero di Thornton Lacey ogni settimana, per tre o quattro ore, se questo lo soddisfacesse. Ma non sarà così. Sa bene che la natura umana ha bisogno di insegnamenti più profondi di quelli che una predica settimanale può fornire; e sa anche che, se non vive tra i suoi parrocchiani e non dimostra con attenzione costante di essere il loro vero amico e protettore, non farà molto né per il loro bene né per il proprio.”

Il signor Crawford acconsentì con un inchino.

“Ripeto ancora una volta,” aggiunse Sir Thomas, “che la casa dei Thornton Lacey è l’unica nel quartiere in cui non mi sentirei a mio agio nell’ospitare il signor Crawford come inquilino.”

Il signor Crawford ringraziò con un inchino.

“Sir Thomas,” disse [[characters/edmund|Edmund]], “indubbiamente comprende il dovere di un prete parrocchiale. Dobbiamo [[concepts/hope|>sperare]] che suo figlio dimostri anche lui di saperlo.”

Qualunque effetto quella breve predica di Sir Thomas potesse realmente avere su Mr. Crawford, suscitò in due delle altre persone presenti sensazioni piuttosto sgradevoli: Miss Crawford e Fanny, le sue ascoltatrici più attente. Una di loro, che prima non aveva mai immaginato che Thornton potesse diventare così rapidamente e completamente la sua “casa”, rifletteva con occhi tristi su ciò che significasse non vedere ogni giorno [[characters/edmund|Edmund]]; l’altra, distolta dalle piacevoli fantasie a cui si era abbandonata sulla base delle descrizioni di suo fratello, non riusciva più, nella visione del futuro che si era fatta di Thornton, a escludere l’idea della chiesa o del clero, e vedeva soltanto una residenza rispettabile, elegante, modernizzata, appartenente a un uomo con mezzi economici indipendenti. Per questo motivo considerava Sir Thomas con profondo disprezzo come il distruttore di tutto ciò, e soffriva ancora di più a causa della riluttanza che il suo carattere e i suoi modi le imponevano, non osando mai sfidarlo o mettere in ridicolo le sue idee.

Tutto il piacere derivante da quella sua speculazione era finito per quell’ora. Era [[motifs/time|ora]] di smettere con le carte, se prevalevano i sermoni; e lei fu felice di scoprire che fosse necessario giungere a una conclusione, e di poter rinfrescare lo spirito cambiando luogo e compagnia.

I capi del gruppo si erano radunati intorno al [[motifs/fire|fuoco]], aspettando la fine della serata. William e Fanny erano i più distaccati dagli altri; rimasero insieme al tavolo da gioco, ormai deserto, chiacchierando tranquillamente senza pensare agli altri, fino a quando alcuni di loro iniziarono a preoccuparsi per loro. La sedia di [[characters/henry-crawford|Henry Crawford]] fu la prima ad essere rivolta verso di loro; lui rimase seduto in silenzio a osservarli per qualche minuto, mentre Sir Thomas, che stava chiacchierando con il dottor Grant, lo osservava a sua volta.

“Questa è la riunione di [[motifs/night|notte]]”, disse William. “Se fossi a Portsmouth, probabilmente ci sarei anch'io.”

“Ma non vorresti trovarti a Portsmouth, William?”

“No, Fanny, non è vero. Ne avrò abbastanza di Portsmouth e delle danze, quando non potrò averti con me. E non so nemmeno se andare alle riunioni abbia qualche senso. Potrei anche non trovare nessuno con cui ballare. Le ragazze di Portsmouth disprezzano chiunque non abbia una “commissione” per partecipare. È come se non fossi nemmeno un midshipman. In realtà, non sono nulla. Ricordi i Gregory? Sono diventate ragazze davvero bellissime, ma a malapena parlano con me. Perché Lucy è corteggiata da un tenente.”

“Oh! Che vergogna, che vergogna. Ma non importa, William” (le sue guance ardevano di indignazione mentre parlava). “Non vale la pena preoccuparsene. Non è affatto un segno negativo su di te; è qualcosa che anche i più grandi ammiragli hanno sperimentato, più o meno, nel corso della loro [[motifs/time|carriera]]. Devi considerarlo una delle difficoltà che toccano a ogni marinaio, come il cattivo tempo e le condizioni di vita dure. Solo con questo vantaggio: tutto finirà, arriverà un [[motifs/time|momento]] in cui non dovrai più sopportare nulla del genere. Quando diventerai tenente. Pensaci, William: quando sarai tenente, non ti importerà affatto di queste sciocchezze.”

“Comincio a pensare che non diventerò mai tenente, Fanny… Tutti riescono tranne me.”

“Oh, caro William, non parlare così; non essere così disperato. Mio zio non dice nulla, ma sono sicura che farà tutto il possibile per farti avere quello che desideri. Lui sa, proprio come te, di quanto sia importante.”

Vedendo suo zio molto più vicino a loro di quanto avesse sospettato, entrambi ritennero necessario parlare di qualcos’altro.

“Ti piace ballare, Fanny?”

“Sì, molto… solo che presto mi stanco.”

“Mi piacerebbe andare a un ballo con te e vederti [[motifs/dance|ballare]]. Non ci sono mai balli a Northampton? Vorrei davvero vederti [[motifs/dance|ballare]], e io ballerei con te se tu lo volessi. Nessuno saprebbe chi sono qui, e mi piacerebbe essere di nuovo il tuo partner. Un tempo ballavamo insieme molte volte, vero? Quando c’era l’organo a mani per strada. So ballare abbastanza bene, ma credo che tu sia ancora migliore.” Poi, rivolgendosi al suo zio che si era avvicinato a loro, aggiunse: “Non è forse Fanny una ballerina molto brava, signore?”

Fanny, disperata di fronte a una domanda del genere senza precedenti, non sapeva dove guardare né come prepararsi alla risposta. Qualsiasi rimprovero molto [[motifs/grave|serio]] o, almeno, l’espressione più fredda di indifferenza avrebbe sicuramente angosciato suo fratello e distrutto lei. Invece, la risposta fu semplicemente: “Mi dispiace dirlo, ma non sono in grado di rispondere alla tua domanda. Non ho mai visto Fanny [[motifs/dance|danzare]] da quando era una bambina; tuttavia, credo che entrambi riconosceremo che si comporta come una vera signorina quando la vedremo, e forse avremo presto l’opportunità di farlo.”

“Ho avuto il piacere di vedere vostra sorella danzare, signor Price,” disse [[characters/henry-crawford|Henry Crawford]], chinandosi in avanti, “e sarò felice di rispondere a qualsiasi domanda voi possiate pormi sull’argomento, per vostro pieno soddisfazione. Ma credo” (notando che Fanny sembrava turbata) “che sia meglio farlo in un altro momento. C’è una persona presente che non gradisce che si parli di Miss Price.”

Infatti, una volta l'aveva vista ballare, Fanny; ed era altrettanto vero che ora avrebbe potuto descrivere con precisione i suoi movimenti agili e eleganti, eseguiti con grande maestria e in tempi impeccabili. Ma in realtà non riusciva assolutamente a ricordare com'era il suo modo di ballare; anzi, dava per scontato che fosse stata lì, senza ricordare nulla di preciso su di lei.

Tuttavia, veniva scambiato per un ammiratore della sua danza; e Sir Thomas, affatto compiaciuto, prolungò la conversazione sul ballo in generale. Era così impegnato a descrivere i balli di Antigua e ad ascoltare ciò che suo nipote poteva raccontargli sui diversi stili di danza che aveva osservato, che non si accorse nemmeno dell’annuncio del suo arrivo in carrozza; fu solo il trambusto causato dalla signora Norris a farglielo notare.

“Ma che fai, Fanny, Fanny. Stiamo per partire! Non vedi che tua zia sta andando via? Sbrigati, non posso permettere che il buon vecchio Wilcox aspetti ancora. Dovresti sempre ricordarti del cocchiere e dei cavalli. Mio caro Sir Thomas, abbiamo già deciso che la carrozza tornerà a prendervi voi, insieme a [[characters/edmund|Edmund]] e William.”

Sir Thomas non poteva dissentire, poiché si trattava di un accordo che lui stesso aveva preso in precedenza, comunicandolo poi a sua moglie e a sua sorella; ma sembrava che la signora Norris lo avesse dimenticato, probabilmente ritenendo di aver risolto tutto da sola.

L’ultima sensazione che provò Fanny durante quella visita fu delusione: il scialle che [[characters/edmund|Edmund]] stava silenziosamente prendendo dal servitore per metterglielo sulle spalle fu afferrato prima da lui dalla mano più veloce del signor Crawford, e lei si trovò costretta ad essere grata alla sua maggiore attenzione.



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_26--part_01" data-title="Mansfield Park — Chapter 26 (part 1)" data-chapter="Chapter 26" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="motif/cross,motif/dance,motif/desire,motif/home,motif/night,motif/silence,motif/time,motif/well,concept/conscience,concept/doubt,concept/hope,concept/unattainable,setting/london,character/bertram,character/edmund,character/julia"></span>


CHAPTER XXVI


William’s [[motifs/desire|desire]] of seeing Fanny [[motifs/dance|dance]] made more than a momentary
impression on his uncle. The [[concepts/hope|hope]] of an opportunity, which Sir Thomas
had then given, was not given to be thought of no more. He remained
steadily inclined to gratify so amiable a feeling; to gratify anybody
else who might wish to see Fanny [[motifs/dance|dance]], and to give pleasure to the
young people in general; and having thought the matter over, and taken
his resolution in quiet independence, the result of it appeared the
next morning at breakfast, when, after recalling and commending what
his nephew had said, he added, “I do not like, William, that you should
leave Northamptonshire without this indulgence. It would give me
pleasure to see you both [[motifs/dance|dance]]. You spoke of the balls at Northampton.
Your cousins have occasionally attended them; but they would not
altogether suit us now. The fatigue would be too much for your aunt. I
believe we must not think of a Northampton ball. A [[motifs/dance|dance]] at [[motifs/home|home]] would
be more eligible; and if—”

“Ah, my dear Sir Thomas!” interrupted Mrs. Norris, “I knew what was
coming. I knew what you were going to say. If dear [[characters/julia|Julia]] were at [[motifs/home|home]],
or dearest Mrs. Rushworth at Sotherton, to afford a reason, an occasion
for such a thing, you would be tempted to give the young people a [[motifs/dance|dance]]
at Mansfield. I know you would. If _they_ were at [[motifs/home|home]] to grace the
ball, a ball you would have this very Christmas. Thank your uncle,
William, thank your uncle!”

“My daughters,” replied Sir Thomas, gravely interposing, “have their
pleasures at Brighton, and I [[concepts/hope|hope]] are very happy; but the [[motifs/dance|dance]] which I
think of giving at Mansfield will be for their cousins. Could we be all
assembled, our satisfaction would undoubtedly be more complete, but the
absence of some is not to debar the others of amusement.”

Mrs. Norris had not another word to say. She saw decision in his looks,
and her surprise and vexation required some minutes’ [[motifs/silence|silence]] to be
settled into composure. A ball at such a [[motifs/time|time]]! His daughters absent and
herself not consulted! There was comfort, however, soon at hand. _She_
must be the doer of everything: Lady [[characters/bertram|Bertram]] would of course be spared
all thought and exertion, and it would all fall upon _her_. She should
have to do the honours of the evening; and this reflection quickly
restored so much of her good-humour as enabled her to join in with the
others, before their happiness and thanks were all expressed.

[[characters/edmund|Edmund]], William, and Fanny did, in their different ways, look and speak
as much grateful pleasure in the promised ball as Sir Thomas could
[[motifs/desire|desire]]. [[characters/edmund|Edmund]]’s feelings were for the other two. His father had never
conferred a favour or shewn a kindness more to his satisfaction.

Lady [[characters/bertram|Bertram]] was perfectly quiescent and contented, and had no
objections to make. Sir Thomas engaged for its giving her very little
trouble; and she assured him “that she was not at all afraid of the
trouble; indeed, she could not imagine there would be any.”

Mrs. Norris was ready with her suggestions as to the rooms he would
think fittest to be used, but found it all prearranged; and when she
would have conjectured and hinted about the day, it appeared that the
day was settled too. Sir Thomas had been amusing himself with shaping a
very complete outline of the business; and as soon as she would listen
quietly, could read his list of the families to be invited, from whom
he calculated, with all necessary allowance for the shortness of the
notice, to collect young people enough to form twelve or fourteen
couple: and could detail the considerations which had induced him to
fix on the 22nd as the most eligible day. William was required to be at
Portsmouth on the 24th; the 22nd would therefore be the last day of his
visit; but where the days were so few it would be unwise to fix on any
earlier. Mrs. Norris was obliged to be satisfied with thinking just the
same, and with having been on the point of proposing the 22nd herself,
as by far the best day for the purpose.

The ball was now a settled thing, and before the evening a proclaimed
thing to all whom it concerned. Invitations were sent with despatch,
and many a young lady went to bed that [[motifs/night|night]] with her head full of
happy cares as [[motifs/well|well]] as Fanny. To her the cares were sometimes almost
beyond the happiness; for young and inexperienced, with small means of
choice and no confidence in her own taste, the “how she should be
dressed” was a point of painful solicitude; and the almost solitary
ornament in her possession, a very pretty amber [[motifs/cross|cross]] which William had
brought her from Sicily, was the greatest distress of all, for she had
nothing but a bit of ribbon to fasten it to; and though she had worn it
in that manner once, would it be allowable at such a [[motifs/time|time]] in the midst
of all the rich ornaments which she supposed all the other young ladies
would appear in? And yet not to wear it! William had wanted to buy her
a gold chain too, but the purchase had been beyond his means, and
therefore not to wear the [[motifs/cross|cross]] might be mortifying him. These were
anxious considerations; enough to sober her spirits even under the
prospect of a ball given principally for her gratification.

The preparations meanwhile went on, and Lady [[characters/bertram|Bertram]] continued to sit
on her sofa without any inconvenience from them. She had some extra
visits from the housekeeper, and her maid was rather hurried in making
up a new dress for her: Sir Thomas gave orders, and Mrs. Norris ran
about; but all this gave _her_ no trouble, and as she had foreseen,
“there was, in fact, no trouble in the business.”

[[characters/edmund|Edmund]] was at this [[motifs/time|time]] particularly full of cares: his mind being
deeply occupied in the consideration of two important events now at
hand, which were to fix his fate in life—ordination and
matrimony—events of such a serious character as to make the ball, which
would be very quickly followed by one of them, appear of less moment in
his eyes than in those of any other person in the house. On the 23rd he
was going to a friend near Peterborough, in the same situation as
himself, and they were to receive ordination in the course of the
Christmas week. Half his destiny would then be determined, but the
other half might not be so very smoothly wooed. His duties would be
established, but the wife who was to share, and animate, and reward
those duties, might yet be [[concepts/unattainable|unattainable]]. He knew his own mind, but he
was not always perfectly assured of knowing Miss Crawford’s. There were
points on which they did not quite agree; there were moments in which
she did not seem propitious; and though trusting altogether to her
affection, so far as to be resolved—almost resolved—on bringing it to a
decision within a very short [[motifs/time|time]], as soon as the variety of business
before him were arranged, and he knew what he had to offer her, he had
many anxious feelings, many doubting hours as to the result. His
conviction of her regard for him was sometimes very strong; he could
look back on a long course of encouragement, and she was as perfect in
disinterested attachment as in everything else. But at other times
[[concepts/doubt|doubt]] and alarm intermingled with his hopes; and when he thought of her
acknowledged disinclination for privacy and retirement, her decided
preference of a [[settings/london|London]] life, what could he expect but a determined
rejection? unless it were an acceptance even more to be deprecated,
demanding such sacrifices of situation and employment on his side as
[[concepts/conscience|conscience]] must forbid.


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

CAPITOLO XXVI


Il [[motifs/desire|desiderio]] di William di veder [[motifs/dance|ballare]] Fanny fece sullo zio un'impressione più che momentanea. La [[concepts/hope|speranza]] di un'occasione, che Sir Thomas aveva allora concesso, non era stata concessa perché non vi si pensasse più. Egli rimase fermamente disposto ad assecondare un sentimento così amabile; a compiacere chiunque altro desiderasse veder [[motifs/dance|ballare]] Fanny, e a dar piacere ai giovani in generale; e avendo riflettuto sulla cosa, e presa la sua decisione in tranquilla indipendenza, il risultato apparve la mattina seguente a colazione, quando, dopo aver richiamato e lodato ciò che il nipote aveva detto, aggiunse: «Non mi piace, William, che tu lasci il Northamptonshire senza questa soddisfazione. Mi farebbe piacere vedervi [[motifs/dance|ballare]] entrambi. Hai parlato dei balli di Northampton. Le tue cugine vi hanno assistito qualche volta; ma ora non farebbero affatto al caso nostro. La fatica sarebbe eccessiva per tua zia. Credo che non dobbiamo pensare a un ballo a Northampton. Una [[motifs/dance|danza]] in [[motifs/home|casa]] sarebbe più opportuna; e se—»

«Ah, mio caro Sir Thomas!» interruppe la signora Norris, «sapevo quel che stava per venire. Sapevo che cosa stavate per dire. Se la cara [[characters/julia|Julia]] fosse in [[motifs/home|casa]], o la carissima signora Rushworth a Sotherton, a fornire una ragione, un'occasione per una cosa simile, sareste tentato di offrire ai giovani una [[motifs/dance|danza]] a Mansfield. So che lo fareste. Se _loro_ fossero in [[motifs/home|casa]] a far bella la festa, un ballo l'avreste proprio questo Natale. Ringrazia tuo zio, William, ringrazia tuo zio!»

«Le mie figlie», replicò Sir Thomas, interponendosi con gravità, «hanno i loro svaghi a Brighton, e [[concepts/hope|spero]] siano molto felici; ma la [[motifs/dance|danza]] che penso di dare a Mansfield sarà per i loro cugini. Se potessimo essere tutti riuniti, la nostra soddisfazione sarebbe senza dubbio più completa, ma l'assenza di alcuni non deve privare gli altri del divertimento.»

La signora Norris non ebbe altro da dire. Vide la decisione nel suo sguardo, e la sua sorpresa e il suo dispetto richiesero qualche minuto di [[motifs/silence|silenzio]] per comporsi in serenità. Un ballo in un [[motifs/time|momento]] simile! Le figlie assenti e lei non consultata! Vi era però un conforto a portata di mano. _Lei_ doveva essere l'artefice di ogni cosa: Lady [[characters/bertram|Bertram]] sarebbe stata naturalmente risparmiata da ogni pensiero e fatica, e tutto sarebbe ricaduto su di _lei_. Sarebbe toccato a lei fare gli onori della serata; e questa riflessione le restituì tanto del suo buon umore da metterla in grado di unirsi agli altri, prima che la loro felicità e i loro ringraziamenti fossero tutti espressi.

[[characters/edmund|Edmund]], William e Fanny, ciascuno a modo suo, mostrarono nello sguardo e nelle parole tutto il grato piacere per il ballo promesso che Sir Thomas potesse [[motifs/desire|desiderare]]. I sentimenti di [[characters/edmund|Edmund]] erano per gli altri due. Suo padre non aveva mai concesso un favore né mostrato una gentilezza che lo soddisfacesse di più.

Lady [[characters/bertram|Bertram]] era perfettamente quieta e contenta, e non aveva obiezioni da fare. Sir Thomas si impegnò perché la cosa le desse pochissimo disturbo; ed ella gli assicurò «che non aveva affatto paura del disturbo; anzi, non riusciva a immaginare che ve ne fosse alcuno».

La signora Norris era pronta con i suoi suggerimenti circa le stanze che egli avrebbe ritenuto più adatte all'uso, ma trovò che tutto era già predisposto; e quando avrebbe voluto fare congetture e allusioni sul giorno, risultò che anche il giorno era stabilito. Sir Thomas si era divertito a tracciare un abbozzo assai completo della faccenda; e non appena ella volle ascoltare in silenzio, poté leggerle l'elenco delle famiglie da invitare, dalle quali calcolava, con tutte le concessioni necessarie alla brevità del preavviso, di raccogliere giovani a sufficienza per formare dodici o quattordici coppie: e poté esporre le considerazioni che lo avevano indotto a fissare il 22 come il giorno più opportuno. William doveva trovarsi a Portsmouth il 24; il 22 sarebbe dunque stato l'ultimo giorno della sua visita; ma essendo i giorni così pochi, sarebbe stato poco saggio sceglierne uno anteriore. La signora Norris dovette accontentarsi di pensare esattamente lo stesso, e di essere stata sul punto di proporre lei stessa il 22, come di gran lunga il giorno migliore allo scopo.

Il ballo era ormai cosa stabilita, e prima di sera cosa annunciata a tutti gli interessati. Gli inviti furono spediti in fretta, e più di una giovane donna andò a letto quella [[motifs/night|notte]] con la testa piena di felici preoccupazioni, [[motifs/well|proprio]] come Fanny. Per lei le preoccupazioni superavano talvolta quasi la felicità; perché, giovane e inesperta, con scarsi mezzi di scelta e nessuna fiducia nel proprio gusto, il «come dovesse vestirsi» era un punto di dolorosa ansia; e l'ornamento quasi unico che possedeva, una bellissima [[motifs/cross|croce]] d'ambra che William le aveva portato dalla Sicilia, era il maggiore di tutti i suoi crucci, perché non aveva che un pezzetto di nastro per fissarla; e sebbene l'avesse già portata a quel modo una volta, sarebbe stato ammissibile in un'[[motifs/time|occasione]] simile, in mezzo a tutti i ricchi ornamenti con cui immaginava che tutte le altre giovani donne sarebbero comparse? Eppure, non portarla! William avrebbe voluto comprarle anche una catenina d'oro, ma l'acquisto era stato al di sopra dei suoi mezzi, e perciò non portare la [[motifs/cross|croce]] avrebbe potuto mortificarlo. Erano considerazioni angosciose; sufficienti a raffreddarle l'animo perfino di fronte alla prospettiva di un ballo dato principalmente per la sua gioia.

I preparativi intanto proseguivano, e Lady [[characters/bertram|Bertram]] continuava a starsene seduta sul suo divano senza riceverne alcun incomodo. Ebbe qualche visita in più dalla governante, e la sua cameriera fu piuttosto affrettata nel confezionarle un vestito nuovo: Sir Thomas dava ordini e la signora Norris correva di qua e di là; ma tutto questo non dava a _lei_ alcun disturbo, e, come aveva previsto, «non c'era, in effetti, alcun disturbo in quella faccenda».

[[characters/edmund|Edmund]] era in quel [[motifs/time|periodo]] particolarmente carico di pensieri: la sua mente era profondamente occupata dalla considerazione di due eventi importanti ormai imminenti, che avrebbero fissato il suo destino nella vita — l'ordinazione e il matrimonio — eventi di carattere così serio da far apparire il ballo, che sarebbe stato seguito assai presto da uno di essi, di minor rilievo ai suoi occhi che a quelli di chiunque altro in casa. Il 23 sarebbe andato da un amico presso Peterborough, nella sua stessa situazione, e avrebbero ricevuto l'ordinazione nel corso della settimana di Natale. Metà del suo destino sarebbe allora stata decisa, ma l'altra metà forse non si sarebbe lasciata corteggiare tanto agevolmente. I suoi doveri sarebbero stati stabiliti, ma la moglie che doveva condividerli, animarli e ricompensarli poteva ancora essere [[concepts/unattainable|irraggiungibile]]. Conosceva il proprio animo, ma non era sempre perfettamente sicuro di conoscere quello di Miss Crawford. Vi erano punti sui quali non erano del tutto d'accordo; vi erano momenti in cui ella non sembrava propizia; e sebbene si affidasse interamente al suo affetto, tanto da essere risoluto — quasi risoluto — a portare la cosa a una decisione entro brevissimo [[motifs/time|tempo]], non appena fossero sistemate le varie faccende che aveva davanti e sapesse che cosa poteva offrirle, provava molti sentimenti d'ansia, molte ore d'incertezza quanto all'esito. La sua convinzione della stima di lei per lui era talvolta assai forte; poteva ripensare a un lungo corso di incoraggiamenti, ed ella era perfetta nell'attaccamento disinteressato come in ogni altra cosa. Ma altre volte il [[concepts/doubt|dubbio]] e l'allarme si mescolavano alle sue speranze; e quando pensava alla sua dichiarata avversione per la solitudine e il ritiro, alla sua decisa preferenza per una vita a [[settings/london|Londra]], che cosa poteva aspettarsi se non un rifiuto risoluto? a meno che non fosse un'accettazione ancor più da temere, che esigesse da parte sua sacrifici di posizione e di occupazione tali che la [[concepts/conscience|coscienza]] doveva vietare.



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_26--part_02" data-title="Mansfield Park — Chapter 26 (part 2)" data-chapter="Chapter 26" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="motif/chains,motif/cross,motif/journey,motif/love,motif/night,motif/well,concept/fear,concept/hope,concept/longing,concept/pride,setting/london,character/edmund"></span>


The issue of all depended on one question. Did she [[motifs/love|love]] him [[motifs/well|well]] enough
to forego what had used to be essential points? Did she [[motifs/love|love]] him [[motifs/well|well]]
enough to make them no longer essential? And this question, which he
was continually repeating to himself, though oftenest answered with a
“Yes,” had sometimes its “No.”

Miss Crawford was soon to leave Mansfield, and on this circumstance the
“no” and the “yes” had been very recently in alternation. He had seen
her eyes sparkle as she spoke of the dear friend’s letter, which
claimed a long visit from her in [[settings/london|London]], and of the kindness of Henry,
in engaging to remain where he was till January, that he might convey
her thither; he had heard her speak of the pleasure of such a [[motifs/journey|journey]]
with an animation which had “no” in every tone. But this had occurred
on the first day of its being settled, within the first hour of the
burst of such enjoyment, when nothing but the friends she was to visit
was before her. He had since heard her express herself differently,
with other feelings, more chequered feelings: he had heard her tell
Mrs. Grant that she should leave her with regret; that she began to
believe neither the friends nor the pleasures she was going to were
worth those she left behind; and that though she felt she must go, and
knew she should enjoy herself when once away, she was already looking
forward to being at Mansfield again. Was there not a “yes” in all this?

With such matters to ponder over, and arrange, and re-arrange, [[characters/edmund|Edmund]]
could not, on his own account, think very much of the evening which the
rest of the family were looking forward to with a more equal degree of
strong interest. Independent of his two cousins’ enjoyment in it, the
evening was to him of no higher value than any other appointed meeting
of the two families might be. In every meeting there was a [[concepts/hope|hope]] of
receiving farther confirmation of Miss Crawford’s attachment; but the
whirl of a ballroom, perhaps, was not particularly favourable to the
excitement or expression of serious feelings. To engage her early for
the two first dances was all the command of individual happiness which
he felt in his power, and the only preparation for the ball which he
could enter into, in spite of all that was passing around him on the
subject, from morning till [[motifs/night|night]].

Thursday was the day of the ball; and on Wednesday morning Fanny, still
unable to satisfy herself as to what she ought to wear, determined to
seek the counsel of the more enlightened, and apply to Mrs. Grant and
her sister, whose acknowledged taste would certainly bear her
blameless; and as [[characters/edmund|Edmund]] and William were gone to Northampton, and she
had reason to think Mr. Crawford likewise out, she walked down to the
Parsonage without much [[concepts/fear|fear]] of wanting an opportunity for private
discussion; and the privacy of such a discussion was a most important
part of it to Fanny, being more than half-ashamed of her own
solicitude.

She met Miss Crawford within a few yards of the Parsonage, just setting
out to call on her, and as it seemed to her that her friend, though
obliged to insist on turning back, was unwilling to lose her walk, she
explained her business at once, and observed, that if she would be so
kind as to give her opinion, it might be all talked over as [[motifs/well|well]]
without doors as within. Miss Crawford appeared gratified by the
application, and after a moment’s thought, urged Fanny’s returning with
her in a much more cordial manner than before, and proposed their going
up into her room, where they might have a comfortable coze, without
disturbing Dr. and Mrs. Grant, who were together in the drawing-room.
It was just the plan to suit Fanny; and with a great deal of gratitude
on her side for such ready and kind attention, they proceeded indoors,
and upstairs, and were soon deep in the interesting subject. Miss
Crawford, pleased with the appeal, gave her all her best judgment and
taste, made everything easy by her suggestions, and tried to make
everything agreeable by her encouragement. The dress being settled in
all its grander parts—“But what shall you have by way of necklace?”
said Miss Crawford. “Shall not you wear your brother’s [[motifs/cross|cross]]?” And as
she spoke she was undoing a small parcel, which Fanny had observed in
her hand when they met. Fanny acknowledged her wishes and doubts on
this point: she did not know how either to wear the [[motifs/cross|cross]], or to
refrain from wearing it. She was answered by having a small trinket-box
placed before her, and being requested to chuse from among several gold
[[motifs/chains|chains]] and necklaces. Such had been the parcel with which Miss Crawford
was provided, and such the object of her intended visit: and in the
kindest manner she now urged Fanny’s taking one for the [[motifs/cross|cross]] and to
keep for her sake, saying everything she could think of to obviate the
scruples which were making Fanny start back at first with a look of
horror at the proposal.

“You see what a collection I have,” said she; “more by half than I ever
use or think of. I do not offer them as new. I offer nothing but an old
necklace. You must forgive the liberty, and oblige me.”

Fanny still resisted, and from her heart. The gift was too valuable.
But Miss Crawford persevered, and argued the case with so much
affectionate earnestness through all the heads of William and the
[[motifs/cross|cross]], and the ball, and herself, as to be finally successful. Fanny
found herself obliged to yield, that she might not be accused of [[concepts/pride|pride]]
or indifference, or some other littleness; and having with modest
reluctance given her consent, proceeded to make the selection. She
looked and looked, [[concepts/longing|longing]] to know which might be least valuable; and
was determined in her choice at last, by fancying there was one
necklace more frequently placed before her eyes than the rest. It was
of gold, prettily worked; and though Fanny would have preferred a
longer and a plainer chain as more adapted for her purpose, she hoped,
in fixing on this, to be chusing what Miss Crawford least wished to
keep. Miss Crawford smiled her perfect approbation; and hastened to
complete the gift by putting the necklace round her, and making her see
how [[motifs/well|well]] it looked. Fanny had not a word to say against its
becomingness, and, excepting what remained of her scruples, was
exceedingly pleased with an acquisition so very apropos. She would
rather, perhaps, have been obliged to some other person. But this was
an unworthy feeling. Miss Crawford had anticipated her wants with a
kindness which proved her a real friend. “When I wear this necklace I
shall always think of you,” said she, “and feel how very kind you
were.”


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

L'esito di tutto dipendeva da una sola domanda. Lo [[motifs/love|amava]] tanto [[motifs/well|bene]] da rinunciare a ciò che un tempo era stato per lei essenziale? Lo [[motifs/love|amava]] tanto [[motifs/well|bene]] da far sì che quelle cose non fossero più essenziali? E questa domanda, che egli si ripeteva di continuo, benché il più delle volte ricevesse un «Sì», aveva talvolta il suo «No».

Miss Crawford doveva lasciare presto Mansfield, e su questa circostanza il «no» e il «sì» si erano alternati assai di recente. Aveva visto i suoi occhi brillare mentre parlava della lettera della cara amica, che reclamava da lei una lunga visita a [[settings/london|Londra]], e della gentilezza di Henry, che si era impegnato a restare dov'era fino a gennaio per poterla accompagnare colà; l'aveva sentita parlare del piacere di un simile [[motifs/journey|viaggio]] con un'animazione che aveva un «no» in ogni tono. Ma ciò era accaduto il primo giorno in cui la cosa era stata decisa, entro la prima ora di quell'esplosione di gioia, quando non aveva davanti a sé che gli amici cui stava per far visita. Da allora l'aveva sentita esprimersi diversamente, con altri sentimenti, sentimenti più contrastati: l'aveva sentita dire alla signora Grant che l'avrebbe lasciata con rammarico; che cominciava a credere che né gli amici né i piaceri verso cui andava valessero quelli che si lasciava alle spalle; e che, per quanto sentisse di dover partire, e sapesse che si sarebbe divertita una volta lontana, già pregustava di essere di nuovo a Mansfield. Non c'era forse un «sì» in tutto questo?

Con simili questioni su cui rimuginare, ordinare e riordinare, [[characters/edmund|Edmund]] non poteva, per conto suo, pensare molto alla serata che il resto della famiglia attendeva con un interesse assai più uniforme e intenso. A prescindere dal godimento che ne avrebbero tratto le sue due cugine, quella serata non aveva per lui maggior valore di qualsiasi altro incontro combinato fra le due famiglie. In ogni incontro c'era la [[concepts/hope|speranza]] di ricevere un'ulteriore conferma dell'affetto di Miss Crawford; ma il turbinio di una sala da ballo, forse, non era particolarmente favorevole al nascere o all'esprimersi di sentimenti seri. Impegnarla per tempo per le prime due danze era tutto il potere sulla propria felicità che sentisse in suo possesso, e l'unico preparativo per il ballo cui potesse dedicarsi, nonostante tutto ciò che intorno a lui si diceva in proposito, dal mattino alla [[motifs/night|notte]].

Giovedì era il giorno del ballo; e mercoledì mattina Fanny, ancora incapace di decidere che cosa dovesse indossare, si risolse a cercare il consiglio di persone più esperte e a rivolgersi alla signora Grant e a sua sorella, il cui riconosciuto buon gusto l'avrebbe certamente messa al riparo da ogni biasimo; e poiché [[characters/edmund|Edmund]] e William erano andati a Northampton, e aveva ragione di credere che anche il signor Crawford fosse fuori, scese a piedi fino alla canonica senza molto [[concepts/fear|timore]] di non trovare l'occasione per un colloquio privato; e la riservatezza di un simile colloquio era per Fanny una parte importantissima della cosa, essendo più che mezzo vergognosa della propria ansia.

Incontrò Miss Crawford a pochi passi dalla canonica, proprio mentre questa usciva per farle visita, e poiché le parve che l'amica, benché costretta a insistere per tornare indietro, fosse restia a rinunciare alla sua passeggiata, le spiegò subito il motivo della sua venuta e osservò che, se fosse stata tanto gentile da darle il proprio parere, se ne poteva discutere tanto [[motifs/well|bene]] fuori quanto dentro casa. Miss Crawford parve compiaciuta della richiesta e, dopo un momento di riflessione, insistette perché Fanny tornasse con lei in modo assai più cordiale di prima, e propose di salire nella sua stanza, dove avrebbero potuto fare una comoda chiacchierata senza disturbare il dottor Grant e la signora Grant, che erano insieme in salotto. Era proprio il piano che faceva al caso di Fanny; e con molta gratitudine da parte sua per un'attenzione così pronta e gentile, entrarono in casa, salirono al piano di sopra e furono presto immerse nell'interessante argomento. Miss Crawford, lusingata dall'appello, le offrì tutto il suo miglior giudizio e gusto, rese ogni cosa facile con i suoi suggerimenti e cercò di rendere ogni cosa piacevole con i suoi incoraggiamenti. Stabilito l'abito in tutte le sue parti principali—«Ma che cosa porterete come collana?» disse Miss Crawford. «Non porterete la [[motifs/cross|croce]] di vostro fratello?» E mentre parlava stava disfacendo un piccolo pacchetto, che Fanny le aveva visto in mano quando si erano incontrate. Fanny confessò i suoi desideri e i suoi dubbi su questo punto: non sapeva né come portare la [[motifs/cross|croce]], né come astenersi dal portarla. Le fu risposto ponendole davanti una piccola scatola di gioielli e invitandola a scegliere fra diverse [[motifs/chains|catene]] d'oro e collane. Tale era il pacchetto di cui Miss Crawford si era munita, e tale lo scopo della visita che intendeva farle: e nel modo più gentile la esortò ora a prenderne una per la [[motifs/cross|croce]] e a conservarla per amor suo, dicendo tutto ciò che le veniva in mente per vincere gli scrupoli che avevano fatto trasalire Fanny, dapprima con uno sguardo di orrore alla proposta.

«Vedete che raccolta possiedo», disse; «ne ho la metà in più di quante ne adoperi o ne prenda in considerazione. Non ve le offro come nuove. Non vi offro nulla se non una vecchia collana. Dovete perdonarmi la libertà e farmi questo favore.»

Fanny resistette ancora, e di tutto cuore. Il dono era troppo prezioso. Ma Miss Crawford perseverò, e sostenne la sua causa con tanta affettuosa premura, passando in rassegna tutti gli argomenti di William e della [[motifs/cross|croce]], del ballo e di se stessa, da riuscire alla fine vittoriosa. Fanny si vide costretta a cedere, per non essere accusata di [[concepts/pride|orgoglio]] o di indifferenza, o di qualche altra meschinità; e, dato con modesta riluttanza il suo consenso, passò a fare la scelta. Guardò e riguardò, [[concepts/longing|bramando]] sapere quale potesse essere la meno preziosa; e si decise infine nella sua scelta immaginando che una collana le fosse stata messa davanti agli occhi più spesso delle altre. Era d'oro, graziosamente lavorata; e sebbene Fanny avrebbe preferito una catena più lunga e più semplice come più adatta al suo scopo, sperò, fissando la scelta su quella, di prendere ciò che Miss Crawford meno desiderava tenere. Miss Crawford sorrise in segno di piena approvazione; e si affrettò a completare il dono mettendole la collana al collo e facendole vedere come le stesse [[motifs/well|bene]]. Fanny non ebbe una parola da dire contro la sua avvenenza e, a parte quel che restava dei suoi scrupoli, fu estremamente contenta di un acquisto tanto opportuno. Avrebbe forse preferito essere obbligata a qualche altra persona. Ma era un sentimento indegno. Miss Crawford aveva previsto i suoi bisogni con una gentilezza che la dimostrava una vera amica. «Quando porterò questa collana penserò sempre a voi», disse, «e sentirò quanto siete stata gentile.»



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_26--part_03" data-title="Mansfield Park — Chapter 26 (part 3)" data-chapter="Chapter 26" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="archetype/child,motif/desire,motif/home,motif/well"></span>


“You must think of somebody else too, when you wear that necklace,”
replied Miss Crawford. “You must think of Henry, for it was his choice
in the first place. He gave it to me, and with the necklace I make over
to you all the duty of remembering the original giver. It is to be a
family remembrancer. The sister is not to be in your mind without
bringing the brother too.”

Fanny, in great astonishment and confusion, would have returned the
present instantly. To take what had been the gift of another person, of
a brother too, impossible! it must not be! and with an eagerness and
embarrassment quite diverting to her companion, she laid down the
necklace again on its cotton, and seemed resolved either to take
another or none at all. Miss Crawford thought she had never seen a
prettier consciousness. “My dear [[archetypes/child|child]],” said she, laughing, “what are
you afraid of? Do you think Henry will claim the necklace as mine, and
fancy you did not come honestly by it? or are you imagining he would be
too much flattered by seeing round your lovely throat an ornament which
his money purchased three years ago, before he knew there was such a
throat in the world? or perhaps”—looking archly—“you suspect a
confederacy between us, and that what I am now doing is with his
knowledge and at his [[motifs/desire|desire]]?”

With the deepest blushes Fanny protested against such a thought.

“[[motifs/well|Well]], then,” replied Miss Crawford more seriously, but without at all
believing her, “to convince me that you suspect no trick, and are as
unsuspicious of compliment as I have always found you, take the
necklace and say no more about it. Its being a gift of my brother’s
need not make the smallest difference in your accepting it, as I assure
you it makes none in my willingness to part with it. He is always
giving me something or other. I have such innumerable presents from him
that it is quite impossible for me to value or for him to remember
half. And as for this necklace, I do not suppose I have worn it six
times: it is very pretty, but I never think of it; and though you would
be most heartily welcome to any other in my trinket-box, you have
happened to fix on the very one which, if I have a choice, I would
rather part with and see in your possession than any other. Say no more
against it, I entreat you. Such a trifle is not worth half so many
words.”

Fanny dared not make any farther opposition; and with renewed but less
happy thanks accepted the necklace again, for there was an expression
in Miss Crawford’s eyes which she could not be satisfied with.

It was impossible for her to be insensible of Mr. Crawford’s change of
manners. She had long seen it. He evidently tried to please her: he was
gallant, he was attentive, he was something like what he had been to
her cousins: he wanted, she supposed, to cheat her of her tranquillity
as he had cheated them; and whether he might not have some concern in
this necklace—she could not be convinced that he had not, for Miss
Crawford, complaisant as a sister, was careless as a woman and a
friend.

Reflecting and doubting, and feeling that the possession of what she
had so much wished for did not bring much satisfaction, she now walked
[[motifs/home|home]] again, with a change rather than a diminution of cares since her
treading that path before.


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

“Dovete pensare anche a qualcun altro, quando porterete quella collana,” replicò Miss Crawford. “Dovete pensare a Henry, perché in origine fu una sua scelta. La diede a me, e insieme alla collana trasferisco a voi tutto il dovere di ricordare chi per primo la donò. Dev’essere un ricordo di famiglia. La sorella non deve presentarsi alla vostra mente senza portare con sé anche il fratello.”

Fanny, stupita e confusa oltre ogni dire, avrebbe voluto restituire il dono all’istante. Accettare ciò che era stato il regalo di un’altra persona, e per giunta di un fratello, impossibile! non doveva essere! e con una premura e un imbarazzo assai divertenti per la sua compagna, ripose la collana sul suo cotone e parve decisa a prenderne un’altra o a non prenderne affatto. Miss Crawford pensò di non aver mai visto un più grazioso pudore. “Mia cara [[archetypes/child|bambina]],” disse ridendo, “di che cosa avete paura? Credete che Henry reclami la collana come mia, e s’immagini che non ne siate venuta in possesso onestamente? oppure vi figurate che sarebbe troppo lusingato nel vedere intorno al vostro bel collo un ornamento comprato col suo denaro tre anni fa, prima che sapesse che esistesse al mondo un collo simile? o forse”—con aria maliziosa—“sospettate un’intesa fra noi, e che quel che sto facendo ora avvenga a sua saputa e per suo [[motifs/desire|desiderio]]?”

Arrossendo profondamente, Fanny protestò contro un simile pensiero.

“[[motifs/well|Bene]], allora,” replicò Miss Crawford più seriamente, ma senza affatto crederle, “per convincermi che non sospettate alcun inganno, e che siete tanto poco incline a supporre complimenti quanto vi ho sempre trovata, prendete la collana e non parliamone più. Il fatto che sia un dono di mio fratello non deve fare la minima differenza nell’accettarla, poiché vi assicuro che non ne fa alcuna nella mia disposizione a separarmene. Egli mi regala sempre qualcosa. Ho da lui doni così innumerevoli che è del tutto impossibile a me apprezzarne e a lui ricordarne la metà. E quanto a questa collana, non credo di averla portata sei volte: è molto graziosa, ma non ci penso mai; e sebbene sareste di tutto cuore la benvenuta a qualunque altra del mio portagioie, vi è capitato di fissarvi proprio su quella che, potendo scegliere, preferirei cedere e vedere in vostro possesso più di ogni altra. Non dite altro contro di essa, ve ne prego. Una simile inezia non vale nemmeno la metà di tante parole.”

Fanny non osò opporre ulteriore resistenza; e con rinnovati ma meno lieti ringraziamenti accettò di nuovo la collana, poiché negli occhi di Miss Crawford c’era un’espressione di cui non poteva essere soddisfatta.

Le era impossibile non accorgersi del mutamento nei modi del signor Crawford. Lo vedeva da tempo. Cercava evidentemente di piacerle: era galante, era premuroso, era press’a poco quello che era stato con le sue cugine: voleva, supponeva lei, defraudarla della sua tranquillità come aveva defraudato loro; e se non avesse qualche parte anche in questa collana—non riusciva a convincersi che non ne avesse, perché Miss Crawford, compiacente come sorella, era sbadata come donna e come amica.

Riflettendo e dubitando, e sentendo che il possesso di ciò che tanto aveva desiderato non le recava molta soddisfazione, tornò ora verso [[motifs/home|casa]], con un mutamento più che con una diminuzione degli affanni rispetto a quando aveva percorso quel sentiero poco prima.



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_27--part_01" data-title="Mansfield Park — Chapter 27 (part 1)" data-chapter="Chapter 27" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="archetype/shadow,motif/cross,motif/desire,motif/home,motif/love,motif/nature,motif/night,motif/pain,motif/time,motif/well,concept/doubt,concept/friendship,concept/history,concept/hope,concept/longing,concept/nature,form/history,character/edmund"></span>


CHAPTER XXVII


On reaching [[motifs/home|home]] Fanny went immediately upstairs to deposit this
unexpected acquisition, this doubtful good of a necklace, in some
favourite box in the East room, which held all her smaller treasures;
but on opening the door, what was her surprise to find her cousin
[[characters/edmund|Edmund]] there writing at the table! Such a sight having never occurred
before, was almost as wonderful as it was welcome.

“Fanny,” said he directly, leaving his seat and his pen, and meeting
her with something in his hand, “I beg your pardon for being here. I
came to look for you, and after waiting a little while in [[concepts/hope|hope]] of your
coming in, was making use of your inkstand to explain my errand. You
will find the beginning of a note to yourself; but I can now speak my
business, which is merely to beg your acceptance of this little
trifle—a chain for William’s [[motifs/cross|cross]]. You ought to have had it a week
ago, but there has been a delay from my brother’s not being in town by
several days so soon as I expected; and I have only just now received
it at Northampton. I [[concepts/hope|hope]] you will like the chain itself, Fanny. I
endeavoured to consult the simplicity of your taste; but, at any rate,
I know you will be kind to my intentions, and consider it, as it really
is, a token of the [[motifs/love|love]] of one of your oldest friends.”

And so saying, he was hurrying away, before Fanny, overpowered by a
thousand feelings of [[motifs/pain|pain]] and pleasure, could attempt to speak; but
quickened by one sovereign wish, she then called out, “Oh! cousin, stop
a moment, pray stop!”

He turned back.

“I cannot attempt to thank you,” she continued, in a very agitated
manner; “thanks are out of the question. I feel much more than I can
possibly express. Your goodness in thinking of me in such a way is
beyond—”

“If that is all you have to say, Fanny” smiling and turning away again.

“No, no, it is not. I want to consult you.”

Almost unconsciously she had now undone the parcel he had just put into
her hand, and seeing before her, in all the niceness of jewellers’
packing, a plain gold chain, perfectly simple and neat, she could not
help bursting forth again, “Oh, this is beautiful indeed! This is the
very thing, precisely what I wished for! This is the only ornament I
have ever had a [[motifs/desire|desire]] to possess. It will exactly suit my [[motifs/cross|cross]]. They
must and shall be worn together. It comes, too, in such an acceptable
moment. Oh, cousin, you do not know how acceptable it is.”

“My dear Fanny, you feel these things a great deal too much. I am most
happy that you like the chain, and that it should be here in [[motifs/time|time]] for
to-morrow; but your thanks are far beyond the occasion. Believe me, I
have no pleasure in the world superior to that of contributing to
yours. No, I can safely say, I have no pleasure so complete, so
unalloyed. It is without a drawback.”

Upon such expressions of affection Fanny could have lived an hour
without saying another word; but [[characters/edmund|Edmund]], after waiting a moment,
obliged her to bring down her mind from its heavenly flight by saying,
“But what is it that you want to consult me about?”

It was about the necklace, which she was now most earnestly [[concepts/longing|longing]] to
return, and hoped to obtain his approbation of her doing. She gave the
[[concepts/history|history]] of her recent visit, and now her raptures might [[motifs/well|well]] be over;
for [[characters/edmund|Edmund]] was so struck with the circumstance, so delighted with what
Miss Crawford had done, so gratified by such a coincidence of conduct
between them, that Fanny could not but admit the superior power of one
pleasure over his own mind, though it might have its drawback. It was
some [[motifs/time|time]] before she could get his attention to her plan, or any answer
to her demand of his opinion: he was in a reverie of fond reflection,
uttering only now and then a few half-sentences of praise; but when he
did awake and understand, he was very decided in opposing what she
wished.

“Return the necklace! No, my dear Fanny, upon no account. It would be
mortifying her severely. There can hardly be a more unpleasant
sensation than the having anything returned on our hands which we have
given with a reasonable [[concepts/hope|hope]] of its contributing to the comfort of a
friend. Why should she lose a pleasure which she has shewn herself so
deserving of?”

“If it had been given to me in the first instance,” said Fanny, “I
should not have thought of returning it; but being her brother’s
present, is not it fair to suppose that she would rather not part with
it, when it is not wanted?”

“She must not suppose it not wanted, not acceptable, at least: and its
having been originally her brother’s gift makes no difference; for as
she was not prevented from offering, nor you from taking it on that
account, it ought not to prevent you from keeping it. No [[concepts/doubt|doubt]] it is
handsomer than mine, and fitter for a ballroom.”

“No, it is not handsomer, not at all handsomer in its way, and, for my
purpose, not half so fit. The chain will agree with William’s [[motifs/cross|cross]]
beyond all comparison better than the necklace.”

“For one [[motifs/night|night]], Fanny, for only one [[motifs/night|night]], if it _be_ a sacrifice; I am
sure you will, upon consideration, make that sacrifice rather than give
[[motifs/pain|pain]] to one who has been so studious of your comfort. Miss Crawford’s
attentions to you have been—not more than you were justly entitled to—I
am the last person to think that _could_ _be_, but they have been
invariable; and to be returning them with what must have something the
_air_ of ingratitude, though I know it could never have the _meaning_,
is not in your [[concepts/nature|nature]], I am sure. Wear the necklace, as you are engaged
to do, to-morrow evening, and let the chain, which was not ordered with
any reference to the ball, be kept for commoner occasions. This is my
advice. I would not have the [[archetypes/shadow|shadow]] of a coolness between the two whose
intimacy I have been observing with the greatest pleasure, and in whose
characters there is so much general resemblance in true generosity and
natural delicacy as to make the few slight differences, resulting
principally from situation, no reasonable hindrance to a perfect
[[concepts/friendship|friendship]]. I would not have the [[archetypes/shadow|shadow]] of a coolness arise,” he
repeated, his voice sinking a little, “between the two dearest objects
I have on earth.”


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

CAPITOLO XXVII


Arrivata a [[motifs/home|>casa]], Fanny salì immediatamente al piano di sopra per riporre questo inaspettato “tesoro”, quel dubbioso collier, in uno dei suoi cassetti preferiti nella stanza orientale, dove teneva tutti i suoi piccoli tesori; ma aprendo la porta, con quale sorpresa scoprì che suo cugino [[characters/edmund|Edmund]] era lì, a scrivere al tavolo! Una scena del genere, mai accaduta prima, fu quasi altrettanto meravigliosa quanto gradita.

“Fanny,” disse lui senza preamboli, alzandosi dalla sedia e lasciando da parte la penna, “mi scuso per essere qui. Sono venuto a cercarti e, dopo aver aspettato un po’ nella speranza che tu arrivassi, ho utilizzato il tuo calamaio per spiegarti lo scopo della mia visita. Troverai all’inizio una lettera indirizzata a te; ma ora posso esporre direttamente il motivo della mia venuta: vorrei che accettassi questo piccolo dono, un braccialetto per il [[motifs/cross|croce]] di William. Avresti dovuto riceverlo una settimana fa, ma ci sono stati alcuni ritardi a causa del fatto che mio fratello non era in città come previsto; l’ho appena ricevuto a Northampton. Spero che ti piaccia questo braccialetto, Fanny. Ho cercato di rispettare i tuoi gusti semplici e sobri; comunque so che comprenderai le mie intenzioni e lo considererai, come in realtà è, un segno dell’[[motifs/love|amore]] di uno dei tuoi più vecchi amici.”

E così dicendo, si affrettò ad andarsene, prima che Fanny, sopraffatta da mille sentimenti di [[motifs/pain|dolore]] e piacere, potesse provare a parlare; ma spinta da un desiderio forte, gridò: “Oh! cugino, aspetta un momento, ti prego!”

Si girò indietro.

“Non riesco nemmeno a provare a ringraziarti,” continuò lei, in modo molto agitato; “i ringraziamenti sono del tutto fuori luogo. Provo qualcosa di molto più grande di quanto possa esprimere a parole. La tua gentilezza nel pensare a me in questo modo è davvero, oltre ogni descrizione.”

“Se questo è tutto quello che hai da dire, Fanny, ” disse sorridendo, poi si girò di nuovo.

"No, no, non è così… Voglio consultarti."

Quasi inconsciamente, aveva già aperto il pacchetto che lui le aveva appena dato; davanti ai suoi occhi, avvolta nella cura tipica dei gioiellieri, c'era una semplice catena d'oro, perfettamente sobria e ordinata. Non poté fare a meno di esclamare di nuovo: “Oh, è davvero bellissima! È proprio quello che desideravo. È l’unico ornamento che abbia mai desiderato possedere. Si abbina perfettamente al mio [[motifs/cross|croce]]. Devono essere indossati insieme. Arriva anche in un momento così opportuno. Oh, cugina, non sai quanto sia perfetto!”

“Mia cara Fanny, tu senti queste cose in modo eccessivo. Sono molto felice che ti piaccia questa catena, e che arrivi qui in [[motifs/time|tempo]] per domani; ma i tuoi ringraziamenti superano di gran lunga l’occasione. Credimi, non esiste alcuna gioia al mondo più grande di quella di poterti aiutare. No, posso dire con certezza che non esiste alcuna gioia più completa, più pura. È davvero senza alcun difetto.”

Di fronte a tali espressioni d'affetto, Fanny avrebbe potuto trascorrere un’ora senza dire una parola; ma [[characters/edmund|Edmund]], dopo aver atteso per un momento, la costrinse a tornare con i piedi per terra dicendo: “Ma di cosa vuoi parlarmi?”

Si trattava del collare, che ora lei desiderava ardentemente restituire e sperava di ottenere il suo consenso al riguardo. Le raccontò l’[[concepts/history|storia]] della sua recente visita; ormai i suoi entusiasmi potevano benissimo finire, poiché [[characters/edmund|Edmund]] era profondamente colpito da quella situazione, molto compiaciuto di ciò che la signorina Crawford aveva fatto e molto soddisfatto di tale coincidenza nel loro comportamento. Fanny non poté fare a meno di riconoscere il maggiore potere di quel piacere su lui, anche se poteva presentare dei svantaggi. Ci volle un po’ prima che riuscisse ad attirare la sua attenzione sul suo piano o a ottenere una risposta alla sua richiesta di parere: era immerso in profonde riflessioni, esprimendo solo di tanto in tanto qualche frase di lode. Ma quando finalmente si rese conto, fu assolutamente contrario a ciò che lei desiderava.

“Restituisci il collare! No, mia cara Fanny, assolutamente no. Sarebbe terribilmente umiliante per lei. Non può esistere sensazione più sgradevole di ricevere indietro qualcosa che abbiamo dato con la speranza che potesse portare conforto a un amico. Perché dovrebbe perdere una gioia di cui si è dimostrata così degna?”

“Se mi fosse stato dato fin dall’inizio,” disse Fanny, “non avrei mai pensato di restituirlo; ma essendo un regalo del fratello di lei, non è giusto supporre che lei preferisca tenerlo, visto che nessuno lo vuole?”

“Non deve pensare che non sia stato desiderato, o almeno accettabile; inoltre, il fatto che originariamente fosse un regalo di suo fratello non cambia nulla: poiché a lei non è stato impedito di offrirlo, né a te di accettarlo per quel motivo, non dovrebbe impedirti di tenerlo. Non ho [[concepts/doubt|dubbi]] che sia più bello del mio e più adatto per una sala da ballo.”

“No, non è più bello, per niente più bello a suo modo, e, per i miei scopi, nemmeno lontanamente adatto. La catena si abbinerà alla [[motifs/cross|croce]] di William in modo incomparabilmente migliore del collare.”

“Per una sola [[motifs/night|notte]], Fanny, per una sola notte, anche se fosse un sacrificio; sono sicuro che, dopo averci pensato bene, lo farai, piuttosto che causare sofferenza a qualcuno che si è sempre preoccupato tanto del tuo benessere. Le attenzioni di Miss Crawford verso di te non sono state altro che ciò a cui avevi pieno diritto. Sono l’ultima persona ad averne dubbi, ma sono state costanti e incondizionate; rifiutare di ricambiarle con un gesto che potrebbe sembrare ingratitudine, anche se so che non ha alcun vero significato, non è certo nel tuo carattere. Indossa il collare, come hai promesso di fare domani sera, e lascia che la catena, che non è stata ordinata per l’occasione del ballo, venga conservata per occasioni più semplici. Questo è il mio consiglio. Non vorrei assolutamente che sorgesse la minima freddezza tra due persone le cui affinità ho osservato con grande piacere, e i cui caratteri presentano tante somiglianze in termini di generosità e delicatezza naturale, al punto che le poche differenze derivanti principalmente dalla situazione non rappresentino alcun ostacolo a una vera e perfetta [[concepts/friendship|amicizia]]. Non vorrei assolutamente che sorgesse la minima freddezza, tra le due persone più care che abbia al mondo,” ripeté, abbassando leggermente la voce.



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_27--part_02" data-title="Mansfield Park — Chapter 27 (part 2)" data-chapter="Chapter 27" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="motif/cross,motif/dance,motif/journey,motif/love,motif/nature,motif/night,motif/tears,motif/time,concept/ambition,concept/deception,concept/heroism,concept/hope,concept/humility,concept/imagination,concept/nature,concept/self,setting/london,character/bertram,character/edmund,character/queen"></span>


He was gone as he spoke; and Fanny remained to tranquillise herself as
she could. She was one of his two dearest—that must support her. But
the other: the first! She had never heard him speak so openly before,
and though it told her no more than what she had long perceived, it was
a stab, for it told of his own convictions and views. They were
decided. He would marry Miss Crawford. It was a stab, in spite of every
long-standing expectation; and she was obliged to repeat again and
again, that she was one of his two dearest, before the words gave her
any sensation. Could she believe Miss Crawford to deserve him, it would
be—oh, how different would it be—how far more tolerable! But he was
deceived in her: he gave her merits which she had not; her faults were
what they had ever been, but he saw them no longer. Till she had shed
many [[motifs/tears|tears]] over this [[concepts/deception|deception]], Fanny could not subdue her agitation;
and the dejection which followed could only be relieved by the
influence of fervent prayers for his happiness.

It was her intention, as she felt it to be her duty, to try to overcome
all that was excessive, all that bordered on selfishness, in her
affection for [[characters/edmund|Edmund]]. To call or to fancy it a loss, a disappointment,
would be a presumption for which she had not words strong enough to
satisfy her own [[concepts/humility|humility]]. To think of him as Miss Crawford might be
justified in thinking, would in her be insanity. To her he could be
nothing under any circumstances; nothing dearer than a friend. Why did
such an idea occur to her even enough to be reprobated and forbidden?
It ought not to have touched on the confines of her [[concepts/imagination|imagination]]. She
would endeavour to be rational, and to deserve the right of judging of
Miss Crawford’s character, and the privilege of true solicitude for him
by a sound intellect and an honest heart.

She had all the [[concepts/heroism|heroism]] of principle, and was determined to do her
duty; but having also many of the feelings of youth and [[concepts/nature|nature]], let her
not be much wondered at, if, after making all these good resolutions on
the side of [[concepts/self|self]]-government, she seized the scrap of paper on which
[[characters/edmund|Edmund]] had begun writing to her, as a treasure beyond all her hopes,
and reading with the tenderest emotion these words, “My very dear
Fanny, you must do me the favour to accept” locked it up with the
chain, as the dearest part of the gift. It was the only thing
approaching to a letter which she had ever received from him; she might
never receive another; it was impossible that she ever should receive
another so perfectly gratifying in the occasion and the style. Two
lines more prized had never fallen from the pen of the most
distinguished author—never more completely blessed the researches of
the fondest biographer. The enthusiasm of a woman’s [[motifs/love|love]] is even beyond
the biographer’s. To her, the handwriting itself, independent of
anything it may convey, is a blessedness. Never were such characters
cut by any other human being as [[characters/edmund|Edmund]]’s commonest handwriting gave!
This specimen, written in haste as it was, had not a fault; and there
was a felicity in the flow of the first four words, in the arrangement
of “My very dear Fanny,” which she could have looked at for ever.

Having regulated her thoughts and comforted her feelings by this happy
mixture of reason and weakness, she was able in due [[motifs/time|time]] to go down and
resume her usual employments near her aunt [[characters/bertram|Bertram]], and pay her the
usual observances without any apparent want of spirits.

Thursday, predestined to [[concepts/hope|hope]] and enjoyment, came; and opened with more
kindness to Fanny than such [[concepts/self|self]]-willed, unmanageable days often
volunteer, for soon after breakfast a very friendly note was brought
from Mr. Crawford to William, stating that as he found himself obliged
to go to [[settings/london|London]] on the morrow for a few days, he could not help trying
to procure a companion; and therefore hoped that if William could make
up his mind to leave Mansfield half a day earlier than had been
proposed, he would accept a place in his carriage. Mr. Crawford meant
to be in town by his uncle’s accustomary late dinner-hour, and William
was invited to dine with him at the Admiral’s. The proposal was a very
pleasant one to William himself, who enjoyed the idea of travelling
post with four horses, and such a good-humoured, agreeable friend; and,
in likening it to going up with despatches, was saying at once
everything in favour of its happiness and dignity which his [[concepts/imagination|imagination]]
could suggest; and Fanny, from a different motive, was exceedingly
pleased; for the original plan was that William should go up by the
mail from Northampton the following [[motifs/night|night]], which would not have allowed
him an hour’s rest before he must have got into a Portsmouth coach; and
though this offer of Mr. Crawford’s would rob her of many hours of his
company, she was too happy in having William spared from the fatigue of
such a [[motifs/journey|journey]], to think of anything else. Sir Thomas approved of it
for another reason. His nephew’s introduction to Admiral Crawford might
be of service. The Admiral, he believed, had interest. Upon the whole,
it was a very joyous note. Fanny’s spirits lived on it half the
morning, deriving some accession of pleasure from its writer being
himself to go away.

As for the ball, so near at hand, she had too many agitations and fears
to have half the enjoyment in anticipation which she ought to have had,
or must have been supposed to have by the many young ladies looking
forward to the same event in situations more at ease, but under
circumstances of less novelty, less interest, less peculiar
gratification, than would be attributed to her. Miss Price, known only
by name to half the people invited, was now to make her first
appearance, and must be regarded as the [[characters/queen|queen]] of the evening. Who could
be happier than Miss Price? But Miss Price had not been brought up to
the trade of _coming_ _out_; and had she known in what light this ball
was, in general, considered respecting her, it would very much have
lessened her comfort by increasing the fears she already had of doing
wrong and being looked at. To [[motifs/dance|dance]] without much observation or any
extraordinary fatigue, to have strength and partners for about half the
evening, to [[motifs/dance|dance]] a little with [[characters/edmund|Edmund]], and not a great deal with Mr.
Crawford, to see William enjoy himself, and be able to keep away from
her aunt Norris, was the height of her [[concepts/ambition|ambition]], and seemed to
comprehend her greatest possibility of happiness. As these were the
best of her hopes, they could not always prevail; and in the course of
a long morning, spent principally with her two aunts, she was often
under the influence of much less sanguine views. William, determined to
make this last day a day of thorough enjoyment, was out snipe-shooting;
[[characters/edmund|Edmund]], she had too much reason to suppose, was at the Parsonage; and
left alone to bear the worrying of Mrs. Norris, who was [[motifs/cross|cross]] because
the housekeeper would have her own way with the supper, and whom _she_
could not avoid though the housekeeper might, Fanny was worn down at
last to think everything an evil belonging to the ball, and when sent
off with a parting worry to dress, moved as languidly towards her own
room, and felt as incapable of happiness as if she had been allowed no
share in it.


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

Se ne andò mentre parlava; e Fanny rimase lì, cercando di calmarsi come poteva. Era una delle sue due persone più care, quella doveva sostenerla. Ma l’altra, la prima! Non lo aveva mai sentito parlare così apertamente prima d’allora; e anche se quelle parole non le rivelavano nulla di nuovo rispetto a ciò che già sapeva da tempo, fu comunque un colpo durissimo: dimostravano infatti le sue convinzioni e i suoi pensieri reali. Erano decisi, avrebbe sposato la signorina Crawford. Un vero colpo, nonostante tutte le aspettative accumulate negli anni. E Fanny dovette ripetere più volte che era una delle sue due persone più care, prima che quelle parole riuscissero a placare il suo dolore.
