and regarding it as what was meant to be the last, last interview of
[[concepts/friendship|friendship]], and investing her with all the feelings of shame and
wretchedness which Crawford’s sister ought to have known, he had gone
to her in such a state of mind, so softened, so devoted, as made it for
a few moments impossible to Fanny’s fears that it should be the last.
But as he proceeded in his story, these fears were over. She had met
him, he said, with a serious—certainly a serious—even an agitated air;
but before he had been able to speak one intelligible sentence, she had
introduced the subject in a manner which he owned had shocked him. “‘I
heard you were in town,’ said she; ‘I wanted to see you. Let us talk
over this sad business. What can equal the folly of our two relations?’
I could not answer, but I believe my looks spoke. She felt reproved.
Sometimes how quick to feel! With a graver look and voice she then
added, ‘I do not mean to defend Henry at your sister’s expense.’ So she
began, but how she went on, Fanny, is not fit, is hardly fit to be
repeated to you. I cannot recall all her words. I would not dwell upon
them if I could. Their substance was great anger at the _folly_ of
each. She reprobated her brother’s folly in being drawn on by a woman
whom he had never cared for, to do what must lose him the woman he
adored; but still more the folly of poor [[characters/maria|Maria]], in sacrificing such a
situation, plunging into such difficulties, under the idea of being
really loved by a man who had long ago made his indifference clear.
Guess what I must have felt. To hear the woman whom—no harsher name
than folly given! So voluntarily, so freely, so coolly to canvass it!
No reluctance, no horror, no feminine, shall I say, no modest
loathings? This is what the world does. For where, Fanny, shall we find
a woman whom [[concepts/nature|nature]] had so richly endowed? Spoilt, spoilt!”

After a little reflection, he went on with a sort of desperate
calmness. “I will tell you everything, and then have done for ever. She
saw it only as folly, and that folly stamped only by exposure. The want
of common discretion, of caution: his going down to Richmond for the
whole [[motifs/time|time]] of her being at Twickenham; her putting herself in the power
of a servant; it was the detection, in short—oh, Fanny! it was the
detection, not the offence, which she reprobated. It was the imprudence
which had brought things to extremity, and obliged her brother to give
up every dearer plan in order to fly with her.”

He stopt. “And what,” said Fanny (believing herself required to speak),
“what could you say?”

“Nothing, nothing to be understood. I was like a man stunned. She went
on, began to talk of you; yes, then she began to talk of you,
regretting, as [[motifs/well|well]] she might, the loss of such a—. There she spoke
very rationally. But she has always done justice to you. ‘He has thrown
away,’ said she, ‘such a woman as he will never see again. She would
have fixed him; she would have made him happy for ever.’ My dearest
Fanny, I am giving you, I [[concepts/hope|hope]], more pleasure than [[motifs/pain|pain]] by this
retrospect of what might have been—but what never can be now. You do
not wish me to be silent? If you do, give me but a look, a word, and I
have done.”

No look or word was given.

“Thank God,” said he. “We were all disposed to [[concepts/wonder|wonder]], but it seems to
have been the merciful appointment of [[concepts/providence|Providence]] that the heart which
knew no guile should not suffer. She spoke of you with high praise and
warm affection; yet, even here, there was alloy, a dash of evil; for in
the midst of it she could exclaim, ‘Why would not she have him? It is
all her fault. Simple girl! I shall never forgive her. Had she accepted
him as she ought, they might now have been on the point of [[motifs/marriage|marriage]],
and Henry would have been too happy and too busy to want any other
object. He would have taken no pains to be on terms with Mrs. Rushworth
again. It would have all ended in a regular standing flirtation, in
yearly meetings at Sotherton and Everingham.’ Could you have believed
it possible? But the charm is broken. My eyes are opened.”

“Cruel!” said Fanny, “quite cruel. At such a moment to give way to
gaiety, to speak with lightness, and to you! Absolute cruelty.”

“Cruelty, do you call it? We differ there. No, hers is not a cruel
[[concepts/nature|nature]]. I do not consider her as meaning to wound my feelings. The evil
lies yet deeper: in her total ignorance, unsuspiciousness of there
being such feelings; in a perversion of mind which made it natural to
her to treat the subject as she did. She was speaking only as she had
been used to hear others speak, as she imagined everybody else would
speak. Hers are not faults of temper. She would not voluntarily give
unnecessary [[motifs/pain|pain]] to any one, and though I may deceive myself, I cannot
but think that for me, for my feelings, she would—. Hers are faults of
principle, Fanny; of blunted delicacy and a corrupted, vitiated mind.
Perhaps it is best for me, since it [[motifs/leaves|leaves]] me so little to regret. Not
so, however. Gladly would I submit to all the increased [[motifs/pain|pain]] of losing
her, rather than have to think of her as I do. I told her so.”

“Did you?”

“Yes; when I left her I told her so.”

“How long were you together?”

“Five-and-twenty minutes. [[motifs/well|Well]], she went on to say that what remained
now to be done was to bring about a [[motifs/marriage|marriage]] between them. She spoke of
it, Fanny, with a steadier voice than I can.” He was obliged to pause
more than once as he continued. “‘We must persuade Henry to marry her,’
said she; ‘and what with [[concepts/honour|honour]], and the certainty of having shut
himself out for ever from Fanny, I do not [[concepts/despair|despair]] of it. Fanny he must
give up. I do not think that even _he_ could now [[concepts/hope|hope]] to succeed with
one of her stamp, and therefore I [[concepts/hope|hope]] we may find no insuperable
difficulty. My influence, which is not small shall all go that way; and
when once married, and properly supported by her own family, people of
respectability as they are, she may recover her footing in society to a
certain degree. In some circles, we know, she would never be admitted,
but with good dinners, and large parties, there will always be those
who will be glad of her acquaintance; and there is, undoubtedly, more
liberality and candour on those points than formerly. What I advise is,
that your father be quiet. Do not let him injure his own cause by
interference. Persuade him to let things take their course. If by any
officious exertions of his, she is induced to leave Henry’s protection,
there will be much less chance of his marrying her than if she remain
with him. I know how he is likely to be influenced. Let Sir Thomas
trust to his [[concepts/honour|honour]] and compassion, and it may all end [[motifs/well|well]]; but if he
get his daughter away, it will be destroying the chief hold.’”


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

Come ascoltava Fanny, con quanta curiosità e preoccupazione, con quale dolore e gioia. Come osservava l’agitazione nella sua voce, e come fissava attentamente ogni oggetto tranne lui stesso. Si può immaginare. L’inizio della storia era allarmante: aveva visto la signorina Crawford, gli era stato chiesto di andarla a trovare, aveva ricevuto una lettera dalla lady Stornaway che lo invitava a farlo; e considerandola l’ultima occasione per un incontro con quella che era stata la sua migliore amica, aveva raggiunto lei in uno stato d’animo profondamente commosso e devoto. Per qualche momento, quindi, le paure di Fanny che si trattasse davvero dell’ultimo incontro erano svanite. Ma man mano che lui continuava a raccontare, quelle paure tornarono. Lei lo aveva accolto con un’espressione seria, anzi, addirittura agitata; ma prima ancora che potesse pronunciare una parola comprensibile, lei aveva affrontato l’argomento in modo che lo aveva scioccato. “Ho sentito che eri in città,” gli aveva detto; “volevo vederti. Parliamo di questa triste situazione. Che follia è stata quella delle nostre due famiglie, ” Non era riuscito a rispondere, ma credo che il suo sguardo parlasse da solo. Lei si era sentita rimproverata. A volte, come si è rapidi nel provare certe emozioni! Con un’espressione e una voce ancora più serie, aveva aggiunto: “Non intendo difendere Henry a scapito di tua sorella, ” E così aveva iniziato. Ma come aveva continuato. Fanny, non è certo il caso che te lo ripeta. Non riesco a ricordare tutte le sue parole. E nemmeno vorrei soffermarmici. Il succo del discorso era una grande rabbia verso la follia di entrambe le famiglie. Lei aveva condannato l’errore di suo fratello, che si era lasciato influenzare da una donna di cui non gli importava nulla, facendo qualcosa che avrebbe perso per sempre la donna che amava; ma ancora di più aveva condannato l’errore della povera Maria, che aveva sacrificato tutto per un uomo che da tempo le aveva dimostrato chiaramente il proprio disinteresse. Immagina cosa abbia provato io. Ascoltare quella donna, che, con tanta volontà, libertà e freddezza, parlava di cose così dolorose. Senza esitazione, senza orrore, senza alcun segno di riluttanza o modestia. Questo è ciò che fa il mondo. Ma dove, Fanny, possiamo trovare una donna a cui la natura abbia donato tali qualità? Corrotta, corrotta.

Dopo un breve momento di riflessione, continuò con una sorta di calma disperata: “Vi dirò tutto, e poi sarà finita per sempre. Lei considerava quella situazione soltanto come una follia, una follia che poteva essere scoperta solo se veniva rivelata. La mancanza di discrezione, la leggerezza con cui lui si recava a Richmond proprio nel periodo in cui lei era a Twickenham; il fatto che lei si mettesse nelle mani di un servitore. In breve, fu proprio la scoperta di tutto ciò – oh, Fanny! – e non il reato stesso, che lei condannò. Fu l’imprudenza a portare le cose a questo estremo, costringendo suo fratello ad abbandonare tutti i suoi progetti più importanti pur di fuggire con lei.”

Si fermò. “E allora,” disse Fanny (convinta di dover parlare),  
“cosa avresti potuto dire?”

“Niente, nulla da capire. Ero come un uomo stordito. Lei continuò a parlare di te; sì, iniziò proprio a parlare di te, rammaricandosi, per quanto potesse farlo, della perdita di una donna del genere. Parlava con grande razionalità. Ma lei ti ha sempre giudicato con equità. ‘Ha gettato via’, disse, ‘una donna come quella che non incontrerà mai più. Lei avrebbe potuto sistemarlo, renderlo felice per sempre, ’ Mia adorata Fanny, spero di farti provare più piacere che dolore ripensando a ciò che avrebbe potuto accadere, ma che ormai non può più accadere. Non vuoi che io rimanga in silenzio? Se sì, dammi solo uno sguardo, una parola, e basterà.”

Nessun sguardo né parola furono scambiati.

“Grazie a Dio,” disse lui. “Eravamo tutti disposti ad [[concepts/wonder|meravigliarci]], ma sembra che sia stata una misericordiosa decisione della [[concepts/providence|Provvidenza]] che quel cuore, privo di ogni malizia, non dovesse soffrire. Lei parlava di te con grande lode e affetto sincero; tuttavia, anche in questo c’era dell’inganno, un pizzico di male. Perché, nonostante tutto, lei riusciva a esclamare: ‘Perché non lo ha preso? È tutta colpa sua. Povera ragazza! Non le perdonerò mai. Se lo avesse accettato come avrebbe dovuto, ora sarebbero probabilmente sposati, e Henry sarebbe stato troppo felice e impegnato per desiderare qualcos’altro. Non si sarebbe nemmeno sforzato di ristabilire i rapporti con la signora Rushworth. Tutto si sarebbe limitato a una relazione superficiale, a incontri annuali a Sotherton ed Everingham, ’ Avresti mai creduto che fosse possibile? Ma ora quel fascino è distrutto. I miei occhi sono finalmente aperti.”

“Crudele!” disse Fanny, “davvero crudele. In un momento del genere cedere alla gioia, parlare con leggerezza, e proprio con te! Una crudeltà assoluta.”

“Crueltà, la chiami così? In questo ci differenziamo. No, la sua non è una natura crudele; non credo che lei abbia intenzione di ferire i miei sentimenti. Il male risiede in qualcosa di più profondo: nella sua totale ignoranza, nella sua mancanza di sospetto riguardo all’esistenza di tali sentimenti; in una distorsione della mente che le rendeva naturale comportarsi nel modo in cui lo ha fatto. Parlava semplicemente come era abituata ad ascoltare gli altri parlare, come immaginava che tutti gli altri parlassero. I suoi non sono difetti di carattere: non infliggerebbe mai volontariamente dolore inutile a nessuno. E anche se potrei ingannarmi, non posso fare a meno di pensare che, per me, per i miei sentimenti, lo farebbe. I suoi sono difetti di principio, Fanny: una delicatezza offuscata e una mente corrotta. Forse è meglio così, visto che questo mi lascia ben poco da rimpiangere. Ma no. Con piacere sopporterei qualsiasi dolore derivante dalla sua perdita, piuttosto che dover pensare a lei in quel modo. Gliel’ho detto.”

"L'hai fatto?"

“Sì; quando l’ho lasciata, gliel’ho detto.”

“Quanto tempo siete stati insieme?”

“Venticinque minuti,” continuò lei. “Ora l’unica cosa da fare è organizzare un [[motifs/marriage|matrimonio]] tra loro. Ne parlava, Fanny, con una voce più ferma di quanto io possa ricordare.” Lui dovette fermarsi più volte mentre proseguiva. “‘Dobbiamo convincere Henry a sposarla,’ disse; ‘e considerando la [[concepts/honour|onore]] e il fatto che ora lui stesso si è escluso per sempre da Fanny, non mi [[concepts/despair|dispero]] del successo. Dovrà rinunciare a lei. Non credo nemmeno che _lui_ possa ora sperare di avere successo con una donna del suo tipo; quindi spero che non incontriamo difficoltà insormontabili. La mia influenza, che non è piccola, sarà utilizzata in questo senso; e una volta sposata e sostenuta dalla sua stessa famiglia, rispettabile com’è, potrà ripristinare una certa posizione nella società. In alcuni ambienti, certo, non verrebbe mai accettata. Ma con buone cene e grandi feste, ci saranno sempre persone disposte ad averla come conoscenza; inoltre, oggi ci sono sicuramente più libertà e sincerità su questi argomenti rispetto al passato. Quello che consiglio è che vostro padre rimanga in silenzio. Non lasciate che interferisca, danneggiando così le proprie possibilità. Convincetelo a lasciare che le cose seguano il loro corso. Se, a causa delle sue intromissioni, lei decidesse di allontanarsi dalla protezione di Henry, le probabilità che lui la sposi diventerebbero molto più scarse rispetto al caso in cui rimanesse con lui. So bene come è facile che venga influenzato. Che Sir Thomas si fidi della sua [[concepts/honour|onore]] e compassione. E tutto potrebbe finire bene. Ma se dovesse portare via sua figlia, significherebbe distruggere la sua unica possibilità di successo.’”



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_47--part_04" data-title="Mansfield Park — Chapter 47 (part 4)" data-chapter="Chapter 47" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="motif/marriage,motif/nature,motif/pain,motif/time,motif/well,concept/friendship,concept/imagination,concept/nature,concept/reconciliation,concept/reform,concept/vanity,character/bertram,character/edmund"></span>


After repeating this, [[characters/edmund|Edmund]] was so much affected that Fanny, watching
him with silent, but most tender concern, was almost sorry that the
subject had been entered on at all. It was long before he could speak
again. At last, “Now, Fanny,” said he, “I shall soon have done. I have
told you the substance of all that she said. As soon as I could speak,
I replied that I had not supposed it possible, coming in such a state
of mind into that house as I had done, that anything could occur to
make me suffer more, but that she had been inflicting deeper wounds in
almost every sentence. That though I had, in the course of our
acquaintance, been often sensible of some difference in our opinions,
on points, too, of some moment, it had not entered my [[concepts/imagination|imagination]] to
conceive the difference could be such as she had now proved it. That
the manner in which she treated the dreadful crime committed by her
brother and my sister (with whom lay the greater seduction I pretended
not to say), but the manner in which she spoke of the crime itself,
giving it every reproach but the right; considering its ill
consequences only as they were to be braved or overborne by a defiance
of decency and impudence in wrong; and last of all, and above all,
recommending to us a compliance, a compromise, an acquiescence in the
continuance of the sin, on the chance of a [[motifs/marriage|marriage]] which, thinking as
I now thought of her brother, should rather be prevented than sought;
all this together most grievously convinced me that I had never
understood her before, and that, as far as related to mind, it had been
the creature of my own [[concepts/imagination|imagination]], not Miss Crawford, that I had been
too apt to dwell on for many months past. That, perhaps, it was best
for me; I had less to regret in sacrificing a [[concepts/friendship|friendship]], feelings,
hopes which must, at any rate, have been torn from me now. And yet,
that I must and would confess that, could I have restored her to what
she had appeared to me before, I would infinitely prefer any increase
of the [[motifs/pain|pain]] of parting, for the sake of carrying with me the right of
tenderness and esteem. This is what I said, the purport of it; but, as
you may imagine, not spoken so collectedly or methodically as I have
repeated it to you. She was astonished, exceedingly astonished—more
than astonished. I saw her change countenance. She turned extremely
red. I imagined I saw a mixture of many feelings: a great, though short
struggle; half a wish of yielding to truths, half a sense of shame, but
habit, habit carried it. She would have laughed if she could. It was a
sort of laugh, as she answered, ‘A pretty good lecture, upon my word.
Was it part of your last sermon? At this rate you will soon [[concepts/reform|reform]]
everybody at Mansfield and Thornton Lacey; and when I hear of you next,
it may be as a celebrated preacher in some great society of Methodists,
or as a missionary into foreign parts.’ She tried to speak carelessly,
but she was not so careless as she wanted to appear. I only said in
reply, that from my heart I wished her [[motifs/well|well]], and earnestly hoped that
she might soon learn to think more justly, and not owe the most
valuable knowledge we could any of us acquire, the knowledge of
ourselves and of our duty, to the lessons of affliction, and
immediately left the room. I had gone a few steps, Fanny, when I heard
the door open behind me. ‘Mr. [[characters/bertram|Bertram]],’ said she. I looked back. ‘Mr.
[[characters/bertram|Bertram]],’ said she, with a smile; but it was a smile ill-suited to the
conversation that had passed, a saucy playful smile, seeming to invite
in order to subdue me; at least it appeared so to me. I resisted; it
was the impulse of the moment to resist, and still walked on. I have
since, sometimes, for a moment, regretted that I did not go back, but I
know I was right, and such has been the end of our acquaintance. And
what an acquaintance has it been! How have I been deceived! Equally in
brother and sister deceived! I thank you for your patience, Fanny. This
has been the greatest relief, and now we will have done.”

And such was Fanny’s dependence on his words, that for five minutes she
thought they _had_ done. Then, however, it all came on again, or
something very like it, and nothing less than Lady [[characters/bertram|Bertram]]’s rousing
thoroughly up could really close such a conversation. Till that
happened, they continued to talk of Miss Crawford alone, and how she
had attached him, and how delightful [[concepts/nature|nature]] had made her, and how
excellent she would have been, had she fallen into good hands earlier.
Fanny, now at liberty to speak openly, felt more than justified in
adding to his knowledge of her real character, by some hint of what
share his brother’s state of health might be supposed to have in her
wish for a complete [[concepts/reconciliation|reconciliation]]. This was not an agreeable
intimation. [[concepts/nature|Nature]] resisted it for a while. It would have been a vast
deal pleasanter to have had her more disinterested in her attachment;
but his [[concepts/vanity|vanity]] was not of a strength to fight long against reason. He
submitted to believe that Tom’s illness had influenced her, only
reserving for himself this consoling thought, that considering the many
counteractions of opposing habits, she had certainly been _more_
attached to him than could have been expected, and for his sake been
more near doing right. Fanny thought exactly the same; and they were
also quite agreed in their opinion of the lasting effect, the indelible
impression, which such a disappointment must make on his mind. [[motifs/time|Time]]
would undoubtedly abate somewhat of his sufferings, but still it was a
sort of thing which he never could get entirely the better of; and as
to his ever meeting with any other woman who could—it was too
impossible to be named but with indignation. Fanny’s [[concepts/friendship|friendship]] was all
that he had to cling to.


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

Dopo aver ripetuto tutto ciò, [[characters/edmund|Edmund]] ne fu così profondamente colpito che Fanny, osservandolo con un silenzio pieno di tenera preoccupazione, quasi si pentì che l’argomento fosse stato affrontato. Trascorse molto tempo prima che potesse parlare di nuovo. Alla fine disse: “Ora, Fanny, sto per finire. Ti ho raccontato sostanzialmente tutto ciò che lei ha detto. Non appena sono riuscito a parlare, le ho risposto che non avrei mai pensato fosse possibile, entrando in quella >casa nello stato d’animo in cui mi trovavo, che potesse accadere qualcosa che mi facesse soffrire ancora di più; ma che lei, con quasi ogni sua frase, stava infliggendomi ferite ancora più profonde. Che, anche se nel corso della nostra conoscenza avevo spesso notato alcune differenze nelle nostre opinioni su alcuni argomenti importanti, non avrei mai immaginato che tali differenze potessero essere così grandi come ora si sono rivelate. Che il modo in cui lei ha trattato il terribile crimine commesso da suo fratello e mia sorella (di cui, a dire il vero, era lei la vera responsabile), nonché il modo in cui ha parlato di quel crimine stesso, attribuendogli ogni tipo di biasimo tranne quello che meritava; considerando le sue conseguenze negative soltanto come qualcosa da affrontare con disprezzo per la decenza e l’impudenza; e soprattutto il fatto che ci ha consigliato di accettare, di comprometterci, di tollerare la continuazione di quel peccato, nella speranza di un [[motifs/marriage|matrimonio]] che, considerando come ora penso a suo fratello, sarebbe meglio evitare piuttosto che cercare. Tutto questo mi ha convinto profondamente che non l’avevo mai veramente compresa prima, e che, per quanto riguarda il suo carattere, era soltanto frutto della mia [[concepts/imagination|immaginazione]], e non la vera Miss Crawford. Che forse era meglio così per me; avrei avuto meno da rimpiangere sacrificando un’[[concepts/friendship|amicizia]], dei sentimenti, delle speranze che ormai erano comunque perduti. Eppure devo ammettere che, se solo fossi riuscito a farle tornare a essere quella che mi era apparsa prima, avrei preferito sopportare qualsiasi aumento del [[motifs/pain|dolore]] della separazione, pur di poter continuare a provare per lei tenerezza e rispetto. Questo è ciò che ho detto. Ma, come puoi immaginare, non l’ho espresso con la stessa chiarezza e sistematicità con cui te lo sto raccontando ora. Lei rimase sbalordita. Molto più di quanto si possa immaginare. Vidi il suo viso cambiare colore; arrossì profondamente. Pensai di vedere un misto di emozioni: una lotta breve ma intensa; metà desiderio di arrendersi alla verità, metà vergogna. Ma fu l’abitudine a prevalere. Avrebbe voluto ridere. Fu una sorta di risata quando rispose: “Che bella ‘lezione’, davvero. Faceva parte del tuo ultimo sermone? A questo ritmo, presto riformerai tutti a Mansfield e Thornton Lacey. E la prossima volta che ti sentirò parlare, forse sarai diventato un famoso predicatore tra i metodisti, o un missionario all’estero, ” Tentò di parlare con noncuranza, ma non ci riuscì del tutto. Risposi soltanto che, dal profondo del cuore, le auguravo il meglio e speravo sinceramente che imparasse presto a pensare in modo più giusto. E poi lasciai la stanza. Avevo fatto pochi passi quando sentii la porta aprirsi dietro di me, “Signor [[characters/bertram|Bertram]]”, disse lei. Mi voltai, “Signor [[characters/bertram|Bertram]]”, ripeté, con un sorriso. Ma era un sorriso inappropriato alle parole appena scambiate. Un sorriso provocatorio, che sembrava volermi sottomettere. Almeno così mi parve. Resistetti. Fu l’impulso del momento. E continuai a camminare. In seguito, a volte, ho rimpianto di non essere tornato indietro. Ma so di aver fatto la cosa giusta. E così è finita la nostra conoscenza. Che strana conoscenza. Quanto sono stato ingannato. Sia riguardo a mio fratello che a mia sorella. Grazie per la tua pazienza, Fanny. Questo mi ha davvero sollevato. Ora possiamo dire di aver finito.”

Fanny era talmente dipendente dalle sue parole che, per cinque minuti, credette davvero che tutto fosse stato fatto. Poi, tuttavia, tutto ricominciò, o qualcosa di molto simile; solo l’intervento deciso di Lady Bertram riuscì a porre fine a quella conversazione. Fino ad allora, continuavano a parlare soltanto di Miss Crawford, di come lei si fosse affezionata a lui, di quanto fosse deliziosa per natura e di quanto sarebbe stata meravigliosa se solo fosse finita nelle giuste mani prima. Ora che Fanny poteva parlare apertamente, ritenne più che giusto fornirgli ulteriori informazioni sul suo vero carattere, accennando anche al fatto che lo stato di salute di suo fratello potesse aver influenzato il suo desiderio di una completa riconciliazione. Questo non fu certo un messaggio piacevole. La natura stessa si oppose per un po’ a tale idea; sarebbe stato molto più confortante se lei fosse stata meno coinvolta in quell’affetto. Ma la sua vanità non fu abbastanza forte da resistere a lungo alla ragione. Accettò l’idea che la malattia di Tom avesse influenzato le sue decisioni, ma si consolò pensando che, considerate le molteplici contraddizioni presenti nelle loro personalità, lei fosse sicuramente stata più legata a lui di quanto ci si potesse aspettare. E che, per amor suo, avesse quasi fatto la cosa giusta. Fanny pensava esattamente lo stesso; erano anche d’accordo sull’effetto duraturo e indelebile che un simile delusione avrebbe avuto sulla sua mente. Il tempo, senza dubbio, avrebbe alleviato in parte i suoi dolori. Ma si trattava comunque di qualcosa da cui non sarebbe mai riuscito a liberarsi completamente. E l’idea che potesse incontrare un’altra donna capace di farlo, beh, era semplicemente impossibile da sopportare. L’unica cosa a cui poteva aggrapparsi era l’amicizia di Fanny.



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_48--part_01" data-title="Mansfield Park — Chapter 48 (part 1)" data-chapter="Chapter 48" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="motif/home,motif/marriage,motif/pain,motif/summer,motif/time,motif/well,concept/education,concept/guilt,concept/hope,concept/humility,concept/melancholy,concept/self,concept/suffering,character/edmund,character/julia,character/maria"></span>


CHAPTER XLVIII


Let other pens dwell on [[concepts/guilt|guilt]] and misery. I quit such odious subjects
as soon as I can, impatient to restore everybody, not greatly in fault
themselves, to tolerable comfort, and to have done with all the rest.

My Fanny, indeed, at this very [[motifs/time|time]], I have the satisfaction of
knowing, must have been happy in spite of everything. She must have
been a happy creature in spite of all that she felt, or thought she
felt, for the distress of those around her. She had sources of delight
that must force their way. She was returned to [[works/mansfield-park-(austen)|Mansfield Park]], she was
useful, she was beloved; she was safe from Mr. Crawford; and when Sir
Thomas came back she had every proof that could be given in his then
[[concepts/melancholy|melancholy]] state of spirits, of his perfect approbation and increased
regard; and happy as all this must make her, she would still have been
happy without any of it, for [[characters/edmund|Edmund]] was no longer the dupe of Miss
Crawford.

It is true that [[characters/edmund|Edmund]] was very far from happy himself. He was
[[concepts/suffering|suffering]] from disappointment and regret, grieving over what was, and
wishing for what could never be. She knew it was so, and was sorry; but
it was with a sorrow so founded on satisfaction, so tending to ease,
and so much in harmony with every dearest sensation, that there are few
who might not have been glad to exchange their greatest gaiety for it.

Sir Thomas, poor Sir Thomas, a parent, and conscious of errors in his
own conduct as a parent, was the longest to suffer. He felt that he
ought not to have allowed the [[motifs/marriage|marriage]]; that his daughter’s sentiments
had been sufficiently known to him to render him culpable in
authorising it; that in so doing he had sacrificed the right to the
expedient, and been governed by motives of selfishness and worldly
wisdom. These were reflections that required some [[motifs/time|time]] to soften; but
[[motifs/time|time]] will do almost everything; and though little comfort arose on Mrs.
Rushworth’s side for the misery she had occasioned, comfort was to be
found greater than he had supposed in his other children. [[characters/julia|Julia]]’s match
became a less desperate business than he had considered it at first.
She was humble, and wishing to be forgiven; and Mr. Yates, desirous of
being really received into the family, was disposed to look up to him
and be guided. He was not very solid; but there was a [[concepts/hope|hope]] of his
becoming less trifling, of his being at least tolerably domestic and
quiet; and at any rate, there was comfort in finding his estate rather
more, and his debts much less, than he had feared, and in being
consulted and treated as the friend best worth attending to. There was
comfort also in Tom, who gradually regained his health, without
regaining the thoughtlessness and selfishness of his previous habits.
He was the better for ever for his illness. He had suffered, and he had
learned to think: two advantages that he had never known before; and
the [[concepts/self|self]]-reproach arising from the deplorable event in Wimpole Street,
to which he felt himself accessory by all the dangerous intimacy of his
unjustifiable theatre, made an impression on his mind which, at the age
of six-and-twenty, with no want of sense or good companions, was
durable in its happy effects. He became what he ought to be: useful to
his father, steady and quiet, and not living merely for himself.

Here was comfort indeed! and quite as soon as Sir Thomas could place
dependence on such sources of good, [[characters/edmund|Edmund]] was contributing to his
father’s ease by improvement in the only point in which he had given
him [[motifs/pain|pain]] before—improvement in his spirits. After wandering about and
sitting under trees with Fanny all the [[motifs/summer|summer]] evenings, he had so [[motifs/well|well]]
talked his mind into submission as to be very tolerably cheerful again.

These were the circumstances and the hopes which gradually brought
their alleviation to Sir Thomas, deadening his sense of what was lost,
and in part reconciling him to himself; though the anguish arising from
the conviction of his own errors in the [[concepts/education|education]] of his daughters was
never to be entirely done away.

Too late he became aware how unfavourable to the character of any young
people must be the totally opposite treatment which [[characters/maria|Maria]] and [[characters/julia|Julia]] had
been always experiencing at [[motifs/home|home]], where the excessive indulgence and
flattery of their aunt had been continually contrasted with his own
severity. He saw how ill he had judged, in expecting to counteract what
was wrong in Mrs. Norris by its reverse in himself; clearly saw that he
had but increased the evil by teaching them to repress their spirits in
his presence so as to make their real disposition unknown to him, and
sending them for all their indulgences to a person who had been able to
attach them only by the blindness of her affection, and the excess of
her praise.

Here had been grievous mismanagement; but, bad as it was, he gradually
grew to feel that it had not been the most direful mistake in his plan
of [[concepts/education|education]]. Something must have been wanting _within_, or [[motifs/time|time]] would
have worn away much of its ill effect. He feared that principle, active
principle, had been wanting; that they had never been properly taught
to govern their inclinations and tempers by that sense of duty which
can alone suffice. They had been instructed theoretically in their
religion, but never required to bring it into daily practice. To be
distinguished for elegance and accomplishments, the authorised object
of their youth, could have had no useful influence that way, no moral
effect on the mind. He had meant them to be good, but his cares had
been directed to the understanding and manners, not the disposition;
and of the necessity of [[concepts/self|self]]-denial and [[concepts/humility|humility]], he feared they had
never heard from any lips that could profit them.

Bitterly did he deplore a deficiency which now he could scarcely
comprehend to have been possible. Wretchedly did he feel, that with all
the cost and care of an anxious and expensive [[concepts/education|education]], he had brought
up his daughters without their understanding their first duties, or his
being acquainted with their character and temper.


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

CAPITOLO XLVIII


Lasciate che altri pensieri si occupino di [[concepts/guilt|colpa]] e miseria. Io evito subito questi argomenti odiosi, impaziente di restituire a tutti coloro che non hanno commesso gravi errori una vita tollerabilmente confortevole, e di liberarmi del resto.

Mia cara Fanny, in effetti, proprio in questo momento, ho la soddisfazione di sapere che lei deve essere stata felice nonostante tutto. Deve essere stata una persona felice, nonostante tutto ciò che provava, o pensava di provare, per il dolore delle persone intorno a lei. Aveva fonti di gioia che inevitabilmente emergevano. È tornata a [[works/mansfield-park-(austen)|Mansfield Park]], era utile, era amata; era al sicuro da Mr. Crawford; e quando Sir Thomas è tornato, ha avuto tutte le prove possibili, considerando lo stato d’animo allora molto malinconico di lui, del suo pieno apprezzamento e della sua crescente stima per lei. E anche se tutto questo doveva renderla felice, lei sarebbe stata comunque felice senza nulla di tutto ciò, perché [[characters/edmund|Edmund]] non era più vittima di Miss Crawford.

È vero che [[characters/edmund|Edmund]] stesso non era affatto felice. Soffriva di delusione e rimorso, si addolorava per ciò che era accaduto e desiderava ciò che non avrebbe mai potuto realizzare. Lei lo sapeva e ne provava dispiacere; ma quel dolore era basato su una sorta di soddisfazione, tendeva a lenire il suo dolore e era in armonia con tutte le sensazioni più preziose per lui. Per questo, pochi probabilmente avrebbero rifiutato di scambiare la propria massima felicità con quel tipo di dolore.

Sir Thomas, povero Sir Thomas. Un genitore che, consapevole degli errori commessi nella propria condotta di genitore, fu il più a soffrire. Sentiva di non aver dovuto permettere quel [[motifs/marriage|matrimonio]]; sapeva bene quali fossero i sentimenti di sua figlia, e questo lo rendeva colpevole per averlo autorizzato; riconosceva di aver sacrificato il giusto per il conveniente, guidato da motivi egoistici e di saggezza mondana. Queste riflessioni richiesero del [[motifs/time|tempo]] per essere superate. Ma il [[motifs/time|tempo]] riesce quasi in tutto; e sebbene la signora Rushworth non trovasse alcun conforto nel dolore che aveva causato, nei suoi altri figli trovò una consolazione maggiore di quanto avesse immaginato. La situazione di [[characters/julia|Julia]] divenne meno disperata di quanto lui avesse ritenuto inizialmente: lei era umile e desiderosa di essere perdonata; il signor Yates, volendo davvero essere accettato nella famiglia, era disposto a rispettarla e a seguirne i consigli. Non era certo una persona molto affidabile, ma c’era la [[concepts/hope|>speranza]] che diventasse meno superficiale, almeno abbastanza serio e tranquillo nel comportamento quotidiano; in ogni caso, era confortante scoprire che le sue proprietà erano migliori e i suoi debiti molto inferiori a quanto temuto. E anche il fatto di essere considerato un amico degno di attenzione rappresentava una grande consolazione. Un altro motivo di sollievo era Tom: gradualmente riprese la salute, senza però tornare alle sue precedenti abitudini sciocche ed egoistiche. Quella malattia lo aveva reso migliore. Aveva sofferto e imparato a riflettere: due vantaggi che prima non possedeva affatto. Inoltre, il senso di colpa derivante dall’evento tragico avvenuto in Wimpole Street – per cui si sentiva in qualche modo responsabile, a causa delle sue relazioni pericolose con quel teatro illegale – ebbe un effetto positivo sulla sua mente. A ventisei anni, senza alcuna mancanza di buon senso o di buoni amici, questi cambiamenti risultarono duraturi. Diventò ciò che avrebbe dovuto essere: utile per suo padre, serio e tranquillo, e non più soltanto interessato a se stesso.

Ecco davvero un conforto! E non appena Sir Thomas poté fare affidamento su tali fonti di bene, [[characters/edmund|Edmund]] iniziò a contribuire al benessere di suo padre migliorando proprio l’unico aspetto che prima gli causava[[motifs/pain|dolore]]: il suo umore. Dopo aver passato tutte le serate estive vagabondando e seduto sotto gli alberi con Fanny, riuscì finalmente a convincersi di accettare la situazione, tornando così a essere abbastanza felice.

Queste furono le circostanze e le speranze che gradualmente portarono un po’ di sollievo a Sir Thomas, attenuando il suo senso di ciò che aveva perso e, in parte, riconciliandolo con se stesso; anche se l’angoscia derivante dalla consapevolezza dei propri errori nell’[[concepts/education|educazione]] delle sue figlie non sarebbe mai completamente scomparsa.

Troppo tardi si rese conto di quanto fosse svantaggioso per il carattere di qualsiasi giovane un trattamento completamente opposto a quello che [[characters/maria|Maria]] e [[characters/julia|Julia]] avevano sempre ricevuto in [[motifs/home|>casa]], dove l’eccessiva indulgenza e i complimenti smisurati della loro zia si contrapponevano costantemente alla sua stessa severità. Capì quanto avesse sbagliato nel pensare di poter compensare gli errori della signora Norris comportandosi al contrario; si rese conto chiaramente che aveva solo peggiorato le cose, insegnando loro a reprimersi in sua presenza per nascondere il vero carattere loro, e mandandole da una persona che riusciva ad attirarle soltanto grazie alla cecità del proprio affetto e ai complimenti eccessivi.

Qui c'era stata una grave mancanza di gestione; ma, per quanto grave fosse, gradualmente iniziò a ritenere che non si trattasse dell'errore più grave nel suo piano di [[concepts/education|educazione]]. Qualcosa doveva esserci mancato _all’interno_ del sistema educativo, altrimenti il tempo avrebbe attenuato gran parte degli effetti negativi. Temeva che quel principio fondamentale – il principio dell’azione concreta e consapevole – fosse stato trascurato; che non fossero mai stati insegnati loro a governare le proprie inclinazioni e i propri temperamenti attraverso quel senso del dovere che, da solo, avrebbe potuto essere sufficiente. Avevano ricevuto istruzioni teoriche sulla loro religione, ma mai veniva richiesto loro di metterle in pratica nella vita quotidiana. Desiderare che fossero eleganti e colti, l’obiettivo ufficiale della loro giovinezza, non poteva avere alcun effetto positivo né influenzarli moralmente. Voleva che diventassero persone buone, ma le sue attenzioni erano state rivolte alla loro intelligenza e ai loro modi di comportarsi, non al loro carattere; inoltre, temeva che non avessero mai sentito parlare della necessità della [[concepts/self|autodisciplina]] e della [[concepts/humility|umiltà]] da labbra capaci di fornire loro un vero insegnamento.

Con amarezza deplorava quella mancanza che ora a malapena riusciva a comprendere come fosse stata possibile. Si sentiva terribilmente consapevole del fatto che, nonostante tutti i costi e le cure dedicate a un’educazione attenta e dispendiosa, aveva cresciuto le sue figlie senza che queste comprendessero i loro primi doveri, né lui conoscesse appieno il loro carattere e il loro temperamento.



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_48--part_02" data-title="Mansfield Park — Chapter 48 (part 2)" data-chapter="Chapter 48" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="motif/home,motif/marriage,motif/spring,motif/tears,motif/time,concept/beauty,concept/education,concept/guilt,concept/hope,concept/melancholy,concept/self,character/henry_crawford,character/julia,character/maria"></span>


The high spirit and strong passions of Mrs. Rushworth, especially, were
made known to him only in their sad result. She was not to be prevailed
on to leave Mr. Crawford. She hoped to marry him, and they continued
together till she was obliged to be convinced that such [[concepts/hope|hope]] was vain,
and till the disappointment and wretchedness arising from the
conviction rendered her temper so bad, and her feelings for him so like
hatred, as to make them for a while each other’s punishment, and then
induce a voluntary separation.

She had lived with him to be reproached as the ruin of all his
happiness in Fanny, and carried away no better consolation in leaving
him than that she _had_ divided them. What can exceed the misery of
such a mind in such a situation?

Mr. Rushworth had no difficulty in procuring a divorce; and so ended a
[[motifs/marriage|marriage]] contracted under such circumstances as to make any better end
the effect of good luck not to be reckoned on. She had despised him,
and loved another; and he had been very much aware that it was so. The
indignities of stupidity, and the disappointments of selfish passion,
can excite little pity. His punishment followed his conduct, as did a
deeper punishment the deeper [[concepts/guilt|guilt]] of his wife. _He_ was released from
the engagement to be mortified and unhappy, till some other pretty girl
could attract him into matrimony again, and he might set forward on a
second, and, it is to be hoped, more prosperous trial of the state: if
duped, to be duped at least with good humour and good luck; while she
must withdraw with infinitely stronger feelings to a retirement and
reproach which could allow no second [[motifs/spring|spring]] of [[concepts/hope|hope]] or character.

Where she could be placed became a subject of most [[concepts/melancholy|melancholy]] and
momentous consultation. Mrs. Norris, whose attachment seemed to augment
with the demerits of her niece, would have had her received at [[motifs/home|home]] and
countenanced by them all. Sir Thomas would not hear of it; and Mrs.
Norris’s anger against Fanny was so much the greater, from considering
_her_ residence there as the motive. She persisted in placing his
scruples to _her_ account, though Sir Thomas very solemnly assured her
that, had there been no young woman in question, had there been no
young person of either sex belonging to him, to be endangered by the
society or hurt by the character of Mrs. Rushworth, he would never have
offered so great an insult to the neighbourhood as to expect it to
notice her. As a daughter, he hoped a penitent one, she should be
protected by him, and secured in every comfort, and supported by every
encouragement to do right, which their relative situations admitted;
but farther than _that_ he could not go. [[characters/maria|Maria]] had destroyed her own
character, and he would not, by a vain attempt to restore what never
could be restored, by affording his sanction to vice, or in seeking to
lessen its disgrace, be anywise accessory to introducing such misery in
another man’s family as he had known himself.

It ended in Mrs. Norris’s resolving to quit Mansfield and devote
herself to her unfortunate [[characters/maria|Maria]], and in an establishment being formed
for them in another country, remote and private, where, shut up
together with little society, on one side no affection, on the other no
judgment, it may be reasonably supposed that their tempers became their
mutual punishment.

Mrs. Norris’s removal from Mansfield was the great supplementary
comfort of Sir Thomas’s life. His opinion of her had been sinking from
the day of his return from Antigua: in every transaction together from
that period, in their daily intercourse, in business, or in chat, she
had been regularly losing ground in his esteem, and convincing him that
either [[motifs/time|time]] had done her much disservice, or that he had considerably
over-rated her sense, and wonderfully borne with her manners before. He
had felt her as an hourly evil, which was so much the worse, as there
seemed no chance of its ceasing but with life; she seemed a part of
himself that must be borne for ever. To be relieved from her,
therefore, was so great a felicity that, had she not left bitter
remembrances behind her, there might have been danger of his learning
almost to approve the evil which produced such a good.

She was regretted by no one at Mansfield. She had never been able to
attach even those she loved best; and since Mrs. Rushworth’s elopement,
her temper had been in a state of such irritation as to make her
everywhere tormenting. Not even Fanny had [[motifs/tears|tears]] for aunt Norris, not
even when she was gone for ever.

That [[characters/julia|Julia]] escaped better than [[characters/maria|Maria]] was owing, in some measure, to a
favourable difference of disposition and circumstance, but in a greater
to her having been less the darling of that very aunt, less flattered
and less spoilt. Her [[concepts/beauty|beauty]] and acquirements had held but a second
place. She had been always used to think herself a little inferior to
[[characters/maria|Maria]]. Her temper was naturally the easiest of the two; her feelings,
though quick, were more controllable, and [[concepts/education|education]] had not given her
so very hurtful a degree of [[concepts/self|self]]-consequence.

She had submitted the best to the disappointment in [[characters/henry-crawford|Henry Crawford]].
After the first bitterness of the conviction of being slighted was
over, she had been tolerably soon in a fair way of not thinking of him
again; and when the acquaintance was renewed in town, and Mr.
Rushworth’s house became Crawford’s object, she had had the merit of
withdrawing herself from it, and of chusing that [[motifs/time|time]] to pay a visit to
her other friends, in order to secure herself from being again too much
attracted. This had been her motive in going to her cousin’s. Mr.
Yates’s convenience had had nothing to do with it. She had been
allowing his attentions some [[motifs/time|time]], but with very little idea of ever
accepting him; and had not her sister’s conduct burst forth as it did,
and her increased dread of her father and of [[motifs/home|home]], on that event,
imagining its certain consequence to herself would be greater severity
and restraint, made her hastily resolve on avoiding such immediate
horrors at all risks, it is probable that Mr. Yates would never have
succeeded. She had not eloped with any worse feelings than those of
selfish alarm. It had appeared to her the only thing to be done.
[[characters/maria|Maria]]’s [[concepts/guilt|guilt]] had induced [[characters/julia|Julia]]’s folly.


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

Lo spirito elevato e le forti passioni della signora Rushworth gli furono resi noti soltanto attraverso i loro tragici risultati. Non fu possibile convincerla ad abbandonare il signor Crawford; sperava di sposarlo, e continuarono a stare insieme fino a quando non dovette riconoscere che tale [[concepts/hope|>speranza]] era vana. La delusione e la disperazione derivanti da questa constatazione resero il suo carattere estremamente cattivo e i suoi sentimenti verso di lui simili all’odio; per un certo periodo, queste emozioni divennero una punizione reciproca, fino a portarli infine a una separazione volontaria.

Aveva vissuto con lui per essere accusata di aver rovinato tutta la sua felicità con Fanny, e non portò con sé, lasciandolo, alcuna consolazione diversa da quella di averli separati. Che cosa può superare la miseria di una mente in tale situazione?

A Mr. Rushworth non fu difficile ottenere il divorzio; e così terminò un [[motifs/marriage|matrimonio]] contratto in circostanze tali che qualsiasi esito migliore sembrava impossibile, anche con la fortuna dalla propria parte. Lei lo disprezzava e amava un altro; lui ne era pienamente consapevole. Le umiliazioni derivanti dall’stupidità e le delusioni causate da passioni egoistiche suscitano ben poca compassione. La sua punizione seguì il suo comportamento, così come una punizione ancora più severa per la [[concepts/guilt|colpa]] ancora maggiore di sua moglie. Lui fu liberato da quell’impegno, ma rimase umiliato e infelice, fino a quando un’altra bella ragazza non lo avrebbe nuovamente attirato nel matrimonio, permettendogli di tentare una seconda volta, e si sperava questa volta più fortunata, esperienza coniugale. Se fosse stato ingannato, almeno lo sarebbe stato con buon umore e fortuna; mentre lei, con sentimenti ancora più profondi, avrebbe dovuto ritirarsi in un’esistenza di rimorso e disprezzo, senza alcuna possibilità di una seconda “primavera” di speranza o di virtù.

Il luogo in cui poteva essere accolta divenne oggetto di profonda [[concepts/melancholy|melanconia]] e di lunghe discussioni. La signora Norris, la cui affezione sembrava crescere con i difetti della sua nipote, avrebbe voluto che lei fosse ospitata a casa loro e accolta da tutti loro. Sir Thomas invece rifiutò categoricamente; l’ira della signora Norris verso Fanny aumentò ancora di più, poiché considerava proprio quella residenza il motivo principale delle sue ostilità. La signora Norris continuò ad attribuire le riserve di Sir Thomas a lei stessa, nonostante lui le assicurasse con grande serietà che, se non ci fosse stata una giovane donna coinvolta, se nessun giovane di entrambi i sessi appartenesse a lui e fosse esposto al pericolo derivante dall’ambiente o dal carattere della signora Rushworth, egli non avrebbe mai offeso così gravemente la comunità locale da sperare che questa ne prendesse nota. Come padre, e soprattutto come uomo desideroso di proteggere una figlia pentita, era disposto a garantirle ogni comodità e incoraggiamento possibile affinché seguisse la retta via; ma non poteva andare oltre. [[characters/maria|Maria]] aveva distrutto il proprio onore e reputazione; lui non avrebbe mai cercato, con tentativi vani, di riparare ciò che era irrimediabilmente perduto, né avrebbe mai dato il proprio sostegno al vizio o cercato di attenuarne le conseguenze negative, permettendo così che una simile sofferenza entrasse nella famiglia di un altro uomo, proprio come lui stesso aveva sperimentato in passato.

Tutto finì con il fatto che la signora Norris decise di lasciare Mansfield e dedicarsi alla sua sfortunata [[characters/maria|Maria]]; in un altro paese, lontano e appartato, fu quindi creato un ambiente adatto a loro. Lì, isolati dal mondo esterno e privi sia di affetto che di giudizio, si può ragionevolmente supporre che il loro carattere divenisse la loro stessa punizione reciproca.

La partenza di Mrs. Norris da Mansfield rappresentò il più grande conforto nella vita di Sir Thomas. Il suo giudizio su di lei era andato peggiorando fin dal giorno del suo ritorno da Antigua: in ogni occasione che avevano condiviso da quel momento, nelle loro conversazioni quotidiane, negli affari o semplicemente durante le chiacchiere, il suo rispetto per lei diminuiva costantemente, convincendolo che o il tempo aveva fatto molto male a lei, oppure che lui aveva sopravvalutato notevolmente i suoi meriti e aveva sopportato con troppa pazienza i suoi modi in passato. La considerava un “male” costante nella sua vita, e la cosa peggiore era che sembrava non esserci alcuna possibilità di liberarsi di lei se non con la morte; lei rappresentava una parte di lui stesso, qualcosa che doveva sopportare per sempre. Pertanto, essere finalmente libero da lei fu una vera felicità. Se solo non avesse lasciato dietro di sé ricordi amari, forse Sir Thomas avrebbe finito per approvare quel “male” che aveva prodotto un risultato così positivo nella sua vita.

A Mansfield, nessuno la rimpiangeva. Non era mai riuscita ad attaccare un legame nemmeno con coloro che amava di più; e da quando la signora Rushworth se n’era andata via, il suo carattere era diventato così irritabile da renderla fonte di tormento ovunque andasse. Nemmeno Fanny versò [[motifs/tears|lacrime]] per zia Norris, nemmeno quando lei se ne andò per sempre.

Il fatto che [[characters/julia|Julia]] fosse riuscita a fuggire meglio di quanto [[characters/maria|Maria]] avesse sperato dipendeva, in parte, da una diversa natura e dalle diverse circostanze; ma soprattutto dal fatto che lei non era la preferita di quella stessa zia, non veniva lusingata né viziata troppo. La sua [[concepts/beauty|bellezza]] e le sue qualità personali occupavano soltanto un secondo posto nel cuore della zia. Era abituata a considerarsi leggermente inferiore a [[characters/maria|Maria]]. Il suo carattere era naturalmente il più mite dei due; i suoi sentimenti, sebbene intensi, erano più facilmente controllabili, e l’[[concepts/education|educazione]] ricevuta non le aveva dato un’eccessiva vanità di sé.

A dispetto della delusione provata nei confronti di [[characters/henry-crawford|Henry Crawford]], aveva comunque inviato il suo miglior lavoro a lui. Dopo che la prima amarezza derivante dall’aver sentito di essere stata offesa era passata, in breve tempo riuscì a smettere del tutto di pensare a lui; quando poi i loro rapporti si ripresero in città e la casa di Mr. Rushworth divenne un obiettivo per Crawford, lei ebbe la prontezza di allontanarsi da quella situazione e scelse proprio quel momento per visitare gli altri suoi amici, al fine di evitare di essere nuovamente troppo attratta da lui. Questo fu il motivo per cui andò a trovare sua cugina; l’opportunità offerta da [[motifs/time|Mr. Yates]] non ebbe alcun ruolo in questa decisione. Per un certo periodo aveva lasciato che lui le dimostrasse interesse, ma senza mai pensare seriamente di accettarlo; se non fosse stato per il comportamento improvviso di sua sorella e per la crescente paura che provava nei confronti di suo padre e della [[motifs/home|casa]], probabilmente Mr. Yates non sarebbe mai riuscito a conquistarla. Lei non era fuggita con sentimenti diversi da quelli di un semplice allarme egoistico; le sembrava l’unica cosa da fare in quella situazione. La [[concepts/guilt|colpa]] di [[characters/maria|Maria]] aveva indotto [[characters/julia|Julia]] a compiere quell’atto sciocco.



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_48--part_03" data-title="Mansfield Park — Chapter 48 (part 3)" data-chapter="Chapter 48" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="motif/death,motif/home,motif/journey,motif/love,motif/marriage,motif/well,concept/ambition,concept/beauty,concept/conscience,concept/doubt,concept/hope,concept/self,concept/temptation,concept/vanity,setting/london,character/bertram,character/edmund,character/fanny_price,character/henry_crawford,character/maria"></span>


[[characters/henry-crawford|Henry Crawford]], ruined by early independence and bad domestic example,
indulged in the freaks of a cold-blooded [[concepts/vanity|vanity]] a little too long. Once
it had, by an opening undesigned and unmerited, led him into the way of
happiness. Could he have been satisfied with the conquest of one
amiable woman’s affections, could he have found sufficient exultation
in overcoming the reluctance, in working himself into the esteem and
tenderness of [[characters/fanny-price|Fanny Price]], there would have been every probability of
success and felicity for him. His affection had already done something.
Her influence over him had already given him some influence over her.
Would he have deserved more, there can be no [[concepts/doubt|doubt]] that more would have
been obtained, especially when that [[motifs/marriage|marriage]] had taken place, which
would have given him the assistance of her [[concepts/conscience|conscience]] in subduing her
first inclination, and brought them very often together. Would he have
persevered, and uprightly, Fanny must have been his reward, and a
reward very voluntarily bestowed, within a reasonable period from
[[characters/edmund|Edmund]]’s marrying Mary.

Had he done as he intended, and as he knew he ought, by going down to
Everingham after his return from Portsmouth, he might have been
deciding his own happy destiny. But he was pressed to stay for Mrs.
Fraser’s party; his staying was made of flattering consequence, and he
was to meet Mrs. Rushworth there. Curiosity and [[concepts/vanity|vanity]] were both
engaged, and the [[concepts/temptation|temptation]] of immediate pleasure was too strong for a
mind unused to make any sacrifice to right: he resolved to defer his
Norfolk [[motifs/journey|journey]], resolved that writing should answer the purpose of it,
or that its purpose was unimportant, and staid. He saw Mrs. Rushworth,
was received by her with a coldness which ought to have been repulsive,
and have established apparent indifference between them for ever; but
he was mortified, he could not bear to be thrown off by the woman whose
smiles had been so wholly at his command: he must exert himself to
subdue so proud a display of resentment; it was anger on Fanny’s
account; he must get the better of it, and make Mrs. Rushworth [[characters/maria|Maria]]
[[characters/bertram|Bertram]] again in her treatment of himself.

In this spirit he began the attack, and by animated perseverance had
soon re-established the sort of familiar intercourse, of gallantry, of
flirtation, which bounded his views; but in triumphing over the
discretion which, though beginning in anger, might have saved them
both, he had put himself in the power of feelings on her side more
strong than he had supposed. She loved him; there was no withdrawing
attentions avowedly dear to her. He was entangled by his own [[concepts/vanity|vanity]],
with as little excuse of [[motifs/love|love]] as possible, and without the smallest
inconstancy of mind towards her cousin. To keep Fanny and the Bertrams
from a knowledge of what was passing became his first object. Secrecy
could not have been more desirable for Mrs. Rushworth’s credit than he
felt it for his own. When he returned from Richmond, he would have been
glad to see Mrs. Rushworth no more. All that followed was the result of
her imprudence; and he went off with her at last, because he could not
help it, regretting Fanny even at the moment, but regretting her
infinitely more when all the bustle of the intrigue was over, and a
very few months had taught him, by the force of contrast, to place a
yet higher value on the sweetness of her temper, the purity of her
mind, and the excellence of her principles.

That punishment, the public punishment of disgrace, should in a just
measure attend _his_ share of the offence is, we know, not one of the
barriers which society gives to virtue. In this world the penalty is
less equal than could be wished; but without presuming to look forward
to a juster appointment hereafter, we may fairly consider a man of
sense, like [[characters/henry-crawford|Henry Crawford]], to be providing for himself no small
portion of vexation and regret: vexation that must rise sometimes to
[[concepts/self|self]]-reproach, and regret to wretchedness, in having so requited
hospitality, so injured family peace, so forfeited his best, most
estimable, and endeared acquaintance, and so lost the woman whom he had
rationally as [[motifs/well|well]] as passionately loved.

After what had passed to wound and alienate the two families, the
continuance of the Bertrams and Grants in such close neighbourhood
would have been most distressing; but the absence of the latter, for
some months purposely lengthened, ended very fortunately in the
necessity, or at least the practicability, of a permanent removal. Dr.
Grant, through an interest on which he had almost ceased to form hopes,
succeeded to a stall in Westminster, which, as affording an occasion
for leaving Mansfield, an excuse for residence in [[settings/london|London]], and an
increase of income to answer the expenses of the change, was highly
acceptable to those who went and those who staid.

Mrs. Grant, with a temper to [[motifs/love|love]] and be loved, must have gone with
some regret from the scenes and people she had been used to; but the
same happiness of disposition must in any place, and any society,
secure her a great deal to enjoy, and she had again a [[motifs/home|home]] to offer
Mary; and Mary had had enough of her own friends, enough of [[concepts/vanity|vanity]],
[[concepts/ambition|ambition]], [[motifs/love|love]], and disappointment in the course of the last half-year,
to be in need of the true kindness of her sister’s heart, and the
rational tranquillity of her ways. They lived together; and when Dr.
Grant had brought on apoplexy and [[motifs/death|death]], by three great institutionary
dinners in one week, they still lived together; for Mary, though
perfectly resolved against ever attaching herself to a younger brother
again, was long in finding among the dashing representatives, or idle
heir-apparents, who were at the command of her [[concepts/beauty|beauty]], and her £20,000,
any one who could satisfy the better taste she had acquired at
Mansfield, whose character and manners could authorise a [[concepts/hope|hope]] of the
domestic happiness she had there learned to estimate, or put [[characters/edmund|Edmund]]
[[characters/bertram|Bertram]] sufficiently out of her head.


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

[[characters/henry-crawford|Henry Crawford]], rovinato dalla precoce indipendenza e da un cattivo esempio familiare, si abbandonò troppo a lungo alle follie di una fredda e spietata [[concepts/vanity|vanità]]. Se solo, per un caso fortuito e ingiustificato, quella vanità lo avesse condotto sulla strada della felicità. Avrebbe potuto accontentarsi di conquistare l’affetto di una donna gentile; avrebbe trovato sufficiente soddisfazione nel superare le sue reticenze e nell’ottenere il rispetto e la tenerezza di [[characters/fanny-price|Fanny Price]]. In quel caso, ogni probabilità di riuscita e felicità sarebbe stata dalla sua parte. Il suo affetto aveva già avuto un certo effetto su di lei; la sua influenza su di lei gli aveva permesso di esercitare a sua volta un ascendente su di lei. Se solo avesse perseverato con onestà. Fanny sarebbe sicuramente diventata sua, e una ricompensa offerta spontaneamente e pienamente volontariamente. Entro un lasso di tempo ragionevole, dopo il matrimonio di [[characters/edmund|Edmund]] con Mary.

Se avesse fatto ciò che intendeva e che sapeva di dover fare, cioè recarsi a Everingham dopo il suo ritorno da Portsmouth, avrebbe potuto decidere da solo il proprio destino felice. Ma fu costretto a rimanere per la festa della signora Fraser; la sua permanenza aveva conseguenze lusinghiere, e inoltre avrebbe incontrato lì la signora Rushworth. La curiosità e la [[concepts/vanity|vanità]] lo spinsero ad agire così; la tentazione del piacere immediato era troppo forte per una mente non abituata a fare sacrifici per il bene: decise quindi di rimandare il suo viaggio a Norfolk, pensando che una lettera potesse servire allo stesso scopo, oppure che tale scopo fosse in realtà irrilevante. Incontrò la signora Rushworth e fu accolto da lei con freddezza; tale comportamento avrebbe dovuto creare un’indifferenza reciproca per sempre. Ma si sentì umiliato: non poteva sopportare di essere respinto da una donna il cui sorriso era stato fino ad allora completamente a sua disposizione. Doveva sforzarsi di superare tale manifestazione di risentimento. Era furioso per Fanny; doveva riuscire a far cambiare atteggiamento alla signora Rushworth nei suoi confronti.

Con questo spirito iniziò l’attacco e, grazie a una perseveranza instancabile, riuscì presto a ripristinare quel tipo di rapporti familiari, di galanteria e di flirtazione che caratterizzavano la loro relazione; ma, vincendo sulla discrezione che, sebbene nata dall’ira, avrebbe potuto salvarli entrambi, si era messo nelle mani di sentimenti da parte sua più forti di quanto avesse immaginato. Lei lo amava; non esisteva alcun modo per allontanare le attenzioni che le erano così care. Lui stesso fu intrappolato dalla propria [[concepts/vanity|vanità]], senza alcuna vera motivazione legata all’[[motifs/love|amore]] e senza mai mostrare la minima incostanza nei confronti della sua cugina. Il suo primo obiettivo divenne quindi impedire a Fanny e ai Bertram di scoprire ciò che stava accadendo. La segretezza era certamente auspicabile per il buon nome della signora Rushworth, proprio come lo era per il suo stesso onore. Quando tornò da Richmond, avrebbe voluto non rivederla mai più. Tutto ciò che seguì fu il risultato della sua imprudenza; alla fine la seguì via perché non poté farne a meno, rimpiangendo Fanny anche in quel momento, ma ancora di più quando tutto lo clamore di quella intrighina si placò e pochi mesi gli fecero comprendere, attraverso il contrasto, quanto fossero preziose la dolcezza del suo carattere, la purezza della sua mente e l’eccellenza dei suoi principi.

Quella punizione, quella pubblica umiliazione, rappresenta, in misura giusta, la conseguenza del suo crimine; sappiamo bene che non costituisce certo uno degli ostacoli che la società pone sul cammino della virtù. In questo mondo, le punizioni sono meno equilibrate di quanto si potrebbe desiderare; ma senza osare prevedere un sistema più giusto in futuro, possiamo considerare che una persona ragionevole, come [[characters/henry-crawford|Henry Crawford]], si sia assicurata per sé una notevole dose di tormento e rimorso: un tormento che a volte si trasforma in autocondanna, e un rimorso che conduce alla disperazione, per aver ricambiato in questo modo l’ospitalità ricevuta, aver turbato la pace familiare, aver perso le persone migliori e più care, e aver perso la donna che amava sia razionalmente che appassionatamente.

Dopo quanto era accaduto, che aveva ferito e allontanato le due famiglie, il continuare a vivere i Bertram e i Grant in un vicinato così stretto sarebbe stato estremamente doloroso; ma l’assenza dei secondi, prolungata intenzionalmente per alcuni mesi, si concluse fortunatamente con la necessità – o almeno con la possibilità pratica – di trasferirsi definitivamente altrove. Il dottor Grant riuscì ad ottenere un negozio a Westminster; questo rappresentava un’opportunità per lasciare Mansfield, una scusa per stabilirsi a [[settings/london|Londra]] e, soprattutto, un aumento dei guadagni sufficiente a coprire le spese del trasloco. Pertanto, questa soluzione fu molto accettabile sia per coloro che se ne andarono sia per quelli che rimasero.

La signora Grant, con un temperamento che anelava all’[[motifs/love|amore]] e ad essere amata, deve essersi separata con qualche rimpianto dalle scene e dalle persone a cui era abituata; ma la stessa felice disposizione d’animo le avrebbe garantito molto di ciò che poteva godere in qualsiasi luogo e in qualsiasi società. Aveva nuovamente un [[motifs/home|casa]] da offrire a Mary; e Mary, dopo aver avuto abbastanza dei propri amici, abbastanza di [[concepts/vanity|vanità]], [[concepts/ambition|ambizione]], [[motifs/love|amore]] e delusioni nell’ultimo semestre, aveva bisogno della vera gentilezza del cuore di sua sorella e della tranquillità razionale delle sue azioni. Vivevano insieme; e quando il dottor Grant morì a causa di tre grandi banchetti organizzati in una settimana, continuarono comunque a vivere insieme. Perché Mary, sebbene fosse fermamente decisa a non legarsi mai più a un fratello minore, impiegò molto tempo per trovare, tra quei giovani affascinanti o eredi oziosi che erano attratti dalla sua [[concepts/beauty|bellezza]] e dai suoi 20.000 sterline, qualcuno che potesse soddisfare i suoi gusti più raffinati, acquisiti a Mansfield. Qualcuno il cui carattere e comportamento potessero far nascere la speranza di una felicità domestica come quella che aveva imparato ad apprezzare lì. O qualcuno che potesse farle dimenticare completamente Edmund e Bertram.



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_48--part_04" data-title="Mansfield Park — Chapter 48 (part 4)" data-chapter="Chapter 48" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="motif/childhood,motif/death,motif/desire,motif/home,motif/love,motif/marriage,motif/road,motif/time,motif/well,concept/hope,concept/poverty,concept/self_deception,concept/truth,character/bertram,character/edmund,character/mary_crawford"></span>


[[characters/edmund|Edmund]] had greatly the advantage of her in this respect. He had not to
wait and wish with vacant affections for an object worthy to succeed
her in them. Scarcely had he done regretting [[characters/mary-crawford|Mary Crawford]], and
observing to Fanny how impossible it was that he should ever meet with
such another woman, before it began to strike him whether a very
different kind of woman might not do just as [[motifs/well|well]], or a great deal
better: whether Fanny herself were not growing as dear, as important to
him in all her smiles and all her ways, as [[characters/mary-crawford|Mary Crawford]] had ever been;
and whether it might not be a possible, a hopeful undertaking to
persuade her that her warm and sisterly regard for him would be
foundation enough for wedded [[motifs/love|love]].

I purposely abstain from dates on this occasion, that every one may be
at liberty to fix their own, aware that the cure of unconquerable
passions, and the transfer of unchanging attachments, must vary much as
to [[motifs/time|time]] in different people. I only entreat everybody to believe that
exactly at the [[motifs/time|time]] when it was quite natural that it should be so, and
not a week earlier, [[characters/edmund|Edmund]] did cease to care about Miss Crawford, and
became as anxious to marry Fanny as Fanny herself could [[motifs/desire|desire]].

With such a regard for her, indeed, as his had long been, a regard
founded on the most endearing claims of innocence and helplessness, and
completed by every recommendation of growing worth, what could be more
natural than the change? Loving, guiding, protecting her, as he had
been doing ever since her being ten years old, her mind in so great a
degree formed by his care, and her comfort depending on his kindness,
an object to him of such close and peculiar interest, dearer by all his
own importance with her than any one else at Mansfield, what was there
now to add, but that he should learn to prefer soft light eyes to
sparkling dark ones. And being always with her, and always talking
confidentially, and his feelings exactly in that favourable state which
a recent disappointment gives, those soft light eyes could not be very
long in obtaining the pre-eminence.

Having once set out, and felt that he had done so on this [[motifs/road|road]] to
happiness, there was nothing on the side of prudence to stop him or
make his progress slow; no doubts of her deserving, no fears of
opposition of taste, no need of drawing new hopes of happiness from
dissimilarity of temper. Her mind, disposition, opinions, and habits
wanted no half-concealment, no [[concepts/self-deception|self-deception]] on the present, no
reliance on future improvement. Even in the midst of his late
infatuation, he had acknowledged Fanny’s mental superiority. What must
be his sense of it now, therefore? She was of course only too good for
him; but as nobody minds having what is too good for them, he was very
steadily earnest in the pursuit of the blessing, and it was not
possible that encouragement from her should be long wanting. Timid,
anxious, doubting as she was, it was still impossible that such
tenderness as hers should not, at times, hold out the strongest [[concepts/hope|hope]] of
success, though it remained for a later period to tell him the whole
delightful and astonishing [[concepts/truth|truth]]. His happiness in knowing himself to
have been so long the beloved of such a heart, must have been great
enough to warrant any strength of language in which he could clothe it
to her or to himself; it must have been a delightful happiness. But
there was happiness elsewhere which no description can reach. Let no
one presume to give the feelings of a young woman on receiving the
assurance of that affection of which she has scarcely allowed herself
to entertain a [[concepts/hope|hope]].

Their own inclinations ascertained, there were no difficulties behind,
no drawback of [[concepts/poverty|poverty]] or parent. It was a match which Sir Thomas’s
wishes had even forestalled. Sick of ambitious and mercenary
connexions, prizing more and more the sterling good of principle and
temper, and chiefly anxious to bind by the strongest securities all
that remained to him of domestic felicity, he had pondered with genuine
satisfaction on the more than possibility of the two young friends
finding their natural consolation in each other for all that had
occurred of disappointment to either; and the joyful consent which met
[[characters/edmund|Edmund]]’s application, the high sense of having realised a great
acquisition in the promise of Fanny for a daughter, formed just such a
contrast with his early opinion on the subject when the poor little
girl’s coming had been first agitated, as [[motifs/time|time]] is for ever producing
between the plans and decisions of mortals, for their own instruction,
and their neighbours’ entertainment.

Fanny was indeed the daughter that he wanted. His charitable kindness
had been rearing a prime comfort for himself. His liberality had a rich
repayment, and the general goodness of his intentions by her deserved
it. He might have made her [[motifs/childhood|childhood]] happier; but it had been an error
of judgment only which had given him the appearance of harshness, and
deprived him of her early [[motifs/love|love]]; and now, on really knowing each other,
their mutual attachment became very strong. After settling her at
Thornton Lacey with every kind attention to her comfort, the object of
almost every day was to see her there, or to get her away from it.

Selfishly dear as she had long been to Lady [[characters/bertram|Bertram]], she could not be
parted with willingly by _her_. No happiness of son or niece could make
her wish the [[motifs/marriage|marriage]]. But it was possible to part with her, because
Susan remained to supply her place. Susan became the stationary niece,
delighted to be so; and equally [[motifs/well|well]] adapted for it by a readiness of
mind, and an inclination for usefulness, as Fanny had been by sweetness
of temper, and strong feelings of gratitude. Susan could never be
spared. First as a comfort to Fanny, then as an auxiliary, and last as
her substitute, she was established at Mansfield, with every appearance
of equal permanency. Her more fearless disposition and happier nerves
made everything easy to her there. With quickness in understanding the
tempers of those she had to deal with, and no natural timidity to
restrain any consequent wishes, she was soon welcome and useful to all;
and after Fanny’s removal succeeded so naturally to her influence over
the hourly comfort of her aunt, as gradually to become, perhaps, the
most beloved of the two. In _her_ usefulness, in Fanny’s excellence, in
William’s continued good conduct and rising fame, and in the general
[[motifs/well|well]]-doing and success of the other members of the family, all
assisting to advance each other, and doing credit to his countenance
and aid, Sir Thomas saw repeated, and for ever repeated, reason to
rejoice in what he had done for them all, and acknowledge the
advantages of early hardship and discipline, and the consciousness of
being born to struggle and endure.

With so much true merit and true [[motifs/love|love]], and no want of fortune and
friends, the happiness of the married cousins must appear as secure as
earthly happiness can be. Equally formed for domestic life, and
attached to country pleasures, their [[motifs/home|home]] was the [[motifs/home|home]] of affection and
comfort; and to complete the picture of good, the acquisition of
Mansfield living, by the [[motifs/death|death]] of Dr. Grant, occurred just after they
had been married long enough to begin to want an increase of income,
and feel their distance from the paternal abode an inconvenience.

On that event they removed to Mansfield; and the Parsonage there,
which, under each of its two former owners, Fanny had never been able
to approach but with some painful sensation of restraint or alarm, soon
grew as dear to her heart, and as thoroughly perfect in her eyes, as
everything else within the view and patronage of [[works/mansfield-park-(austen)|Mansfield Park]] had
long been.

FINIS.


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

[[characters/edmund|Edmund]] aveva un grande vantaggio rispetto a lei in questo senso. Non doveva aspettare né sperare, con sentimenti vuoti e senza oggetto, che qualcuno fosse degno di sostituirla nel suo cuore. Appena iniziò a rimpiangere [[characters/mary-crawford|Mary Crawford]] e a dirlo a Fanny, osservando quanto fosse impossibile incontrare un'altra donna simile, gli venne in mente che forse un tipo di donna molto diverso avrebbe potuto fare esattamente lo stesso, o addirittura molto meglio. Forse Fanny stessa stava diventando per lui sempre più cara e importante, con tutti i suoi sorrisi e i suoi modi, proprio come lo era stata [[characters/mary-crawford|Mary Crawford]]. E forse sarebbe stato possibile, persino promettente, convincerla che il suo affetto caloroso e fraterno nei suoi confronti potesse costituire una base sufficiente per un amore coniugale vero.

In questa occasione mi astengo intenzionalmente da indicare date precise, affinché ognuno possa sceglierne liberamente una a proprio piacimento, consapevole che la cura delle passioni invincibili e il cambiamento degli affetti immutabili dipendono in gran misura dal [[motifs/time|tempo]] e da persona a persona. Vorrei solo chiedere a tutti di credere che esattamente nel momento in cui era del tutto naturale che accadesse, e non una settimana prima, [[characters/edmund|Edmund]] smise di interessarsi a Miss Crawford e divenne altrettanto desideroso di sposare Fanny quanto lo fosse lei stessa.
